META.subject: Essential Mathematics
META.subtitleDoc: CBE Phenomenon-Driven Lesson Sequence — Sub-Strand 3.2 (8 Lessons)

UNIT.subject: Essential Mathematics
UNIT.content:
• Equally likely events: performing experiments involving equally likely outcomes (e.g., tossing a coin, rolling a six-faced die)
• Computing probability of equally likely outcomes
• Range of probability: determining the range of probability of an event (0 to 1)
• Mutually exclusive events: identifying and performing experiments involving mutually exclusive events in real-life situations
• Probability of a single chance event involving mutually exclusive events
• Independent events: performing experiments involving independent events (maximum of two experiments and two outcomes)
• Probability of independent events in different situations
• Application of probability in real-life situations including discussing the dangers of gambling
UNIT.learningOutcomes:
By the end of the sub-strand, the learner should be able to:
a) perform experiments involving equally likely outcomes in different situations,
b) compute probability of equally likely outcomes,
c) determine the range of probability of an event,
d) identify mutually exclusive events in real life situations,
e) perform experiments of single chance involving mutually exclusive events,
f) calculate the probability of an event involving a single chance,
g) perform experiments involving independent events,
h) determine the probability of independent events in different situations,
i) appreciate the role of probability in real-life situations.
UNIT.coreCompetencies:
• Communication and Collaboration: the learner collaborates with peers when evaluating successes and failures from experiments involving mutually exclusive events to work out the probability of possible outcomes, and when sharing results from coin-toss and dice-roll experiments.
• Critical Thinking and Problem Solving: the learner develops interpretation and inference skills when discussing the dangers of gambling using the knowledge of probability, and when determining the range of probability from real-life scenarios such as predicting rainfall in Kisumu or match outcomes for a Nairobi football team.
UNIT.values:
• Responsibility: the learner makes correct and ethical decisions on life issues that involve gambling and chance, using the knowledge of probability to understand risk.
• Unity: the learner collaborates respectfully with others when carrying out probability experiments such as tossing coins, rolling dice, and drawing cards, taking turns and recording results fairly.
UNIT.sep:
• Asking Questions and Defining Problems: learners formulate questions about why outcomes of repeated chance experiments (e.g., tossing a coin 50 times) do not always split exactly 50/50, driving inquiry into theoretical vs. experimental probability.
• Planning and Carrying Out Investigations: learners design and carry out coin-toss, dice-roll, and card-draw experiments, recording outcomes systematically in frequency tables to gather evidence about equally likely, mutually exclusive, and independent events.
• Analysing and Interpreting Data: learners analyse experimental results from repeated trials, compare experimental probability to theoretical probability, and draw conclusions about the range and behaviour of probability values.
• Engaging in Argument from Evidence: learners use probability data to construct arguments about the dangers of gambling, presenting evidence to peers that long-run odds favour the "house" in games of chance.
UNIT.pcis:
• Life Skills (Decision Making): the learner makes informed decisions on real-life issues involving probability, such as understanding the dangers of gambling, assessing risk in sports betting, and evaluating chance in everyday situations common in Kenyan communities.
• Financial Literacy: the learner applies the concept of probability to understand risk and expected value, particularly in the context of gambling and betting activities, reinforcing responsible financial behaviour.
UNIT.careers:
• Insurance and Actuarial Science: probability is foundational to calculating risk, setting premiums, and underwriting policies — careers accessible through institutions such as the Actuarial Society of Kenya.
• Sports Management and Coaching: probability underpins performance analysis, match prediction, and strategic decision-making in Kenyan sports such as athletics, football, and rugby.
• Journalism and Media: journalists and data reporters use probability and statistics to report on polls, elections, health surveys, and sporting odds for Kenyan audiences.
• Hospitality and Tourism Industry: probability concepts inform demand forecasting, overbooking strategies, and risk management in hotels and safari lodges across Kenya's tourism sector.
• Guidance and Counselling: counsellors use probabilistic reasoning to communicate risk (e.g., health risk behaviours, gambling addiction) when advising students and community members.
UNIT.focus: This unit introduces Grade 10 Essential Mathematics learners to the foundational concepts of probability through hands-on experiments, peer discussion, and real-life Kenyan contexts. Learners progress from understanding equally likely outcomes and the probability scale, through identifying and calculating probabilities for mutually exclusive events, to exploring independent events across two experiments with two outcomes. Throughout, the unit foregrounds responsible decision-making — particularly the mathematics behind why gambling is a losing proposition — anchoring abstract probability concepts in situations learners encounter in their communities.
UNIT.phenomenon: During the 2023 Kenyan Premier League season, sports commentators and fans frequently debated whether Gor Mahia FC's winning streak was "bound to end soon" — claiming the team was "due" for a loss after so many consecutive wins. At the same time, betting advertisements across Nairobi matatus and social media told youth that they could predict match outcomes and "beat the odds." Students are presented with this puzzling situation: if each football match is an independent event, why do so many people believe past results change the probability of future ones? And if a coin has landed on heads five times in a row, is tails now more likely? This seemingly simple question — do past outcomes change future chances? — is deeply counterintuitive and opens the door to exploring equally likely events, the range of probability, mutually exclusive events, and the mathematics of independence. The phenomenon is puzzling because everyday language and gambling culture actively promote the gambler's fallacy, yet probability mathematics tells a different story.
UNIT.supportingPhenomena:
• A mandazi vendor in Kericho market tells a customer: "I've flipped this 10-shilling coin six times and it landed tails every time — heads must come next!" Students investigate whether this claim is mathematically valid, using repeated coin-toss experiments to explore equally likely outcomes and the range of probability.
• During a class raffle for a school trip to Lake Victoria, two learners wonder: "If my name is drawn for Prize 1, can it also win Prize 2?" This supports exploration of mutually exclusive versus non-mutually exclusive events and single-chance probability.
• A student notices that the probability of rain on any given day in Kisumu during April (historically ~70%) does not change based on whether it rained the day before. This real Kenyan weather context supports understanding of independent events and how probabilities are combined across two trials.
• A Nairobi school's sports day features a spinner game at the fundraising stall — spin to win a free soda or mandazi. Students analyse the spinner's sections to determine whether the game is fair, connecting equally likely outcomes, range of probability, and the idea that the stall (like a casino) is always designed to win in the long run.
UNIT.drivingQuestion:
DRIVING QUESTION: If past outcomes of a chance event — like a coin toss or a football match — do not change future probabilities, how can we use mathematics to predict what is likely to happen, and why does this understanding protect us from the dangers of gambling?

KICD KEY INQUIRY QUESTION:
1. How do we apply probability in day-to-day life?
UNIT.storylineThread:
Lesson 1 — Anchoring Phenomenon & Equally Likely Events: Learners are introduced to the Gor Mahia / betting-odds phenomenon. They brainstorm what "chance" means in daily life (rain in Kisumu, drawing a card, tossing a coin). Working in pairs, learners toss a 10-shilling coin 40 times, record outcomes in a tally table, and calculate experimental probability of heads and tails. The class pools data and compares results to the theoretical probability of ½. The Driving Question is posted on the Driving Question Board (DQB).

Lesson 2 — Computing Probability of Equally Likely Outcomes: Learners roll a six-faced die 60 times in groups, record outcomes, and compute experimental probabilities for each face. They derive the formula P(event) = number of favourable outcomes ÷ total number of equally likely outcomes. Worked examples use Kenyan contexts: drawing a name from a hat of 30 learners, picking a red ball from a bag of githeri-coloured tokens. Learners update the DQB with new understanding.

Lesson 3 — Range of Probability: Learners investigate the boundaries of probability using real-life Kenyan scenarios — probability that the sun rises tomorrow over Mombasa (certain = 1), probability that it snows in Kisumu in July (impossible = 0), and intermediate cases. They construct a probability number line (0 to 1), place events on it, and write probability statements using fractions, decimals, and percentages. The idea that no experiment can yield P > 1 or P < 0 is formalised. DQB is updated.

Lesson 4 — Mutually Exclusive Events (Identification & Concept): Learners examine the school raffle supporting phenomenon. Through discussion and sorting activities, they identify events that cannot happen simultaneously (mutually exclusive: rolling a 2 AND a 5 on one die; drawing a heart AND a spade in one draw) versus those that can. They list real-life Kenyan examples: a matatu cannot be in Nairobi and Mombasa at the same time; a learner cannot score both an A and a D on the same paper. The addition rule P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) for mutually exclusive events is introduced with guided examples.

Lesson 5 — Probability of Single-Chance Mutually Exclusive Events: Learners carry out experiments with a bag of coloured tokens (representing mandazi flavours: plain, coconut, cardamom) and a single draw. They calculate P(plain OR coconut) using the addition rule. Multiple worked examples are solved: a spinner divided into unequal sectors, a die showing an even OR a 5, selecting a day that is Monday OR Friday from a school week. Learners practise independently and peer-mark. DQB is updated with the addition rule.

Lesson 6 — Independent Events (Concept & Experiments): The Kisumu rainfall supporting phenomenon is used to launch independent events. Learners carry out two-stage experiments: toss a coin AND roll a die; draw a card, replace it, draw again. They list all possible outcomes using tree diagrams and two-way tables (sample space). The rule P(A and B) = P(A) × P(B) for independent events is derived from the data and formalised. Connections back to the DQ: why does a coin NOT "remember" its last result?

Lesson 7 — Probability of Independent Events in Context: Learners apply the multiplication rule to two-experiment, two-outcome scenarios rooted in Kenyan life: probability that it rains on both Monday and Tuesday in Kisumu given daily P(rain) = 0.7; probability that two independently chosen Grade 10 learners are both female given school demographics; probability that a mandazi vendor sells out on two consecutive market days. Learners discuss the spinner/stall supporting phenomenon and calculate why the stall always profits in the long run. Dangers of gambling are discussed using probability evidence. DQB is substantially updated.

Lesson 8 — Consolidation, Model Building & DQB Closure: Learners revisit the anchoring phenomenon (Gor Mahia / betting odds) and use all probability concepts learned to explain mathematically why each match is independent, why the gambler's fallacy is false, and why gambling is designed to be a losing proposition. Groups present mini-posters connecting equally likely events, range of probability, mutually exclusive events, and independent events to the Driving Question. The DQB is reviewed and closed. A class written assessment covers all SLOs; learners also complete a short reflection on one real-life decision they would make differently using probability knowledge.

LESSONS.title: Anchoring Phenomenon & Equally Likely Events: Is Gor Mahia "Due" for a Loss?

slo.purpose: To anchor the unit in the Gor Mahia / sports-betting phenomenon and establish the foundational concept that equally likely events have a fixed theoretical probability regardless of past outcomes.
slo.knowledge: Learners will know that: (a) equally likely outcomes each have the same chance of occurring; (b) theoretical probability of an equally likely event = (number of favourable outcomes) ÷ (total number of possible outcomes); (c) experimental probability is calculated from trials and may differ from theoretical probability; (d) as the number of trials increases, experimental probability approaches theoretical probability (Law of Large Numbers, introduced informally).
slo.skills: Learners will be able to: (a) perform a coin-toss experiment, record outcomes in a tally table, and calculate experimental probability of heads and tails; (b) compare experimental probability to the theoretical probability of ½; (c) pool class data and observe the effect of increasing sample size; (d) articulate in writing why past outcomes of an independent event do NOT change its future probability.
slo.attitudes: Learners will appreciate that mathematics provides an objective tool for evaluating claims about chance, and will begin to develop a critical, evidence-based stance towards gambling advertisements and the gambler's fallacy. (Value: Responsibility — making correct decisions on life issues that involve gambling using the knowledge of probability.)
slo.keyInquiry: How do we apply probability in day-to-day life?
slo.purposeInStoryline: This is the opening lesson of the unit. It anchors all subsequent learning in the real-world Gor Mahia / Nairobi-betting phenomenon. Learners encounter the central puzzle — do past outcomes change future chances? — before any formal instruction, ensuring genuine curiosity. The coin-toss experiment generates personal data that learners will return to throughout the unit as they build increasingly sophisticated probability models. The Driving Question Board (DQB) opened today becomes the living record of the class's growing understanding across all lessons.
slo.safetyNotes: No chemical or physical hazards. Remind learners to handle 10-shilling coins hygienically (wash hands after handling coins). Ensure learners toss coins onto the desk surface — not across the room — to avoid distractions or injury.

LESSONS.overview: In this opening lesson, learners encounter the anchoring phenomenon: during the 2023 Kenyan Premier League season, fans claimed Gor Mahia FC was "due" for a loss after a winning streak, while betting advertisements on Nairobi matatus and social media promised youth they could "beat the odds." Learners first predict whether past results of a coin toss can change the probability of future outcomes. They then conduct a structured coin-toss experiment (40 tosses per pair, using a 10-shilling coin), record outcomes in a tally table, and calculate experimental probability. Class data are pooled to compare experimental results with the theoretical probability of ½. The lesson closes with the formal opening of the Driving Question Board (DQB) and an introductory model sketch connecting the phenomenon to the mathematics of equally likely events. No prior probability knowledge is assumed; this lesson surfaces and challenges everyday misconceptions before formal teaching begins.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners read a short printed or on-screen scenario card (2–3 sentences) describing two situations: (A) Gor Mahia FC has won their last 7 Premier League matches. A fan says, 'They are definitely due for a loss next week — you can't keep winning forever!' (B) A matatu in Nairobi displays a betting-app advert: 'Use our stats — predict the next winner and earn KSh 5,000 today!' Working individually (3 minutes, silent), learners write answers to two prompts in their exercise books: (1) 'Do you agree with the fan? Is Gor Mahia now MORE likely to lose? Explain your thinking.' (2) 'If you toss a 10-shilling coin and it lands on heads five times in a row, is tails now more likely on the sixth toss? Why or why not?' Learners then share with a partner (Think-Pair-Share, 2 minutes). Three to four pairs are cold-called to share their partner's prediction with the class.
framework.teacherMoves: 1. Display or distribute the scenario card. Read it aloud with expression, pausing at the fan's quote. Ask: 'Has anyone seen adverts like this on a matatu or on their phone? What do they promise?' (Allow 2–3 hands, 30 seconds.) 2. Issue the two written prompts. Say exactly: 'Work alone — no talking, no looking at your neighbour's book. I want YOUR honest thinking before we do any maths. You have 3 minutes.' Start a visible timer. 3. After 3 minutes: 'Now share your answer to question 1 with the person next to you. Listen carefully — you will be asked to report your PARTNER'S idea, not your own. 2 minutes.' 4. After pair-share, cold-call exactly 4 pairs using the class register (do not ask for volunteers): 'Amina, tell me what YOUR PARTNER said about Gor Mahia being due for a loss.' WAIT 10 seconds after each name before prompting. Record key student ideas (verbatim) on the board under two columns: 'Past results DO change future chances' vs 'Past results DON'T change future chances.' 5. Do NOT correct misconceptions yet. Say: 'We are going to use mathematics today to find out who is right. Keep your predictions — we will return to them at the end.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Think-Pair-Share with cold-call reporting. This strategy surfaces prior knowledge and misconceptions (especially the gambler's fallacy) before instruction, giving the teacher diagnostic information and creating cognitive dissonance that motivates the investigation. Recording student ideas on the board validates all voices and sets up a public record to revisit.
framework.formativeAssessment: OBSERVABLE INDICATOR: Teacher scans written responses during the 3-minute silent period and notes (on a clipboard or sticky note) how many learners in each row wrote that tails becomes 'more likely' after five heads — this is the key misconception to track. Cold-call responses reveal the depth of reasoning. TARGET: All learners have committed a written prediction to their books before the experiment begins.

framework.learnerExperience: Working in pairs, learners conduct a structured coin-toss experiment. Each pair receives one 10-shilling coin. Learner A tosses the coin; Learner B records the outcome (H or T) using tally marks in a pre-drawn table in their exercise books. They complete 40 tosses, then swap roles to verify. After recording, each pair calculates: (i) Number of Heads, (ii) Number of Tails, (iii) Experimental P(Heads) = (Number of Heads) ÷ 40, (iv) Experimental P(Tails) = (Number of Tails) ÷ 40. Results are written on a sticky note or called out to the class recorder, who fills in a shared class tally table on the board (one row per pair). The class then calculates the pooled totals and pooled experimental probabilities using all pairs' data combined.
framework.teacherMoves: 1. Before distributing coins, say: 'We are going to gather EVIDENCE — just like a scientist at the Kenya Medical Research Institute gathers data before drawing conclusions. Your job is to record every single outcome honestly. No cheating the toss.' 2. Draw the tally table on the board: columns = Toss Number (groups of 5), Outcome (H/T), Running Total H, Running Total T. Say: 'Copy this table NOW. Leave space for 40 rows.' Allow 2 minutes for table setup. 3. Distribute coins. Say: 'Hold the coin at the edge, flip it with your thumb, catch it on the back of your other hand. Do NOT spin it on the desk — that changes the physics.' Demonstrate once. 4. Circulate during the experiment. Every 3–4 minutes, narrate: 'Pair at the back — I can see you have 15 heads out of 20. What is your experimental probability of heads so far? [WAIT 10 seconds.] Does that surprise you?' Ask at least 6 different pairs a similar running-probability question during the activity. 5. After 40 tosses per pair: 'Stop. Calculate your experimental P(Heads) and P(Tails) now. Round to 2 decimal places.' Allow 3 minutes. 6. Call out results pair by pair and fill the class table on the board. Ask the class recorder (a learner) to compute the column totals aloud. Then ask: 'What is our CLASS experimental probability of heads?' Cold-call one learner to compute it on the board. WAIT 15 seconds. 7. Write the theoretical probability: 'Mathematics tells us P(Heads) = 1/2 = 0.50. How does our class result compare?' Pause for reactions.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Pooled Data Aggregation. By combining all pairs' data into a single class table, learners directly observe the Law of Large Numbers informally: as the number of trials increases, experimental probability approaches 0.50. This makes abstract theory tangible and Kenya-grounded (their own coin, their own tosses). It also mirrors how actuaries and insurance companies in Nairobi use large datasets to estimate risk.
framework.formativeAssessment: OBSERVABLE INDICATOR: Each pair's tally table is complete (40 entries, no gaps) and their calculated experimental probability is a decimal between 0 and 1. Teacher checks 6–8 pairs' tables during circulation — look specifically for: (a) correct tally grouping in fives, (b) correct division (e.g., 22 ÷ 40 = 0.55, not 22/40 left as a fraction without simplification). RED FLAG: Any pair whose total H + T ≠ 40 — stop and correct immediately before they submit to the class table.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners return to their original predictions from Phase 1. The teacher facilitates a whole-class discussion connecting the coin-toss data to the Gor Mahia phenomenon. Learners are guided to: (a) define 'equally likely outcomes' using their coin-toss experience; (b) state the formula for theoretical probability of equally likely events: P(event) = (number of favourable outcomes) ÷ (total number of outcomes); (c) apply the formula to: a coin toss (P(H) = 1/2), rolling a fair die (P(3) = 1/6 — introduced as an extension example), and the Gor Mahia match scenario (is a football match an equally likely event?). Learners write a structured 'Explanation Paragraph' in their exercise books (individual, 5 minutes): 'The fan said Gor Mahia was due for a loss. Using what we learned today, I can explain that…'
framework.teacherMoves: 1. Point to the two columns on the board from Phase 1. Say: 'Look at what you predicted before the experiment. Now look at our data. What does the evidence tell us?' Cold-call 3 learners — one from each prediction column and one who left a 'not sure' response. WAIT 12 seconds each time. 2. Ask: 'If we tossed this coin another 40 times, would it REMEMBER the results from the first 40 tosses?' WAIT 10 seconds. Take 2 responses. Then say firmly: 'A coin has no memory. Each toss is a fresh, independent event. The mathematics does not change.' Write on the board: 'Each toss is INDEPENDENT. Past outcomes do NOT change future probability.' 3. Introduce the formula. Say: 'In mathematics we define: P(event) = number of favourable outcomes ÷ total number of equally likely outcomes. For our coin: P(Heads) = 1 ÷ 2 = 0.5. Always. After 5 heads in a row — still 0.5.' Write this on the board with a box around it. 4. Ask: 'Now think about Gor Mahia. Is a football match the same as a coin toss? Are all outcomes equally likely?' WAIT 15 seconds. Take 3 responses. Guide learners to notice that football matches involve skill, fitness, home advantage — they are NOT simple equally likely events. Say: 'We will explore this deeper in later lessons. For now, write your explanation paragraph.' 5. After 5 minutes of individual writing, cold-call 2 learners to read their paragraph. Offer specific praise: 'Excellent — Fatuma used the word INDEPENDENT correctly.' Correct any learner who writes 'tails was more likely' with a direct, calm restatement: 'Evidence shows P(Heads) stayed close to 0.5 throughout. The coin does not know what it did before.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Claim-Evidence-Reasoning (CER) Writing Frame. Learners construct an explanation paragraph using the structure: Claim (the fan is wrong) → Evidence (our coin-toss data, theoretical formula) → Reasoning (each toss is independent; past outcomes don't change P). This NGSS Science and Engineering Practice (Constructing Explanations) bridges the concrete experiment to the abstract mathematical principle and directly dismantles the gambler's fallacy.
framework.formativeAssessment: OBSERVABLE INDICATOR: The explanation paragraph must contain three elements to be assessed as 'Meets Expectations': (1) a correct statement of the probability formula, (2) use of the word 'independent' or 'does not change,' (3) a direct reference back to the coin experiment or Gor Mahia scenario. Teacher reads 4–6 paragraphs as learners write (circulate and read over shoulders). Mark a small tick on the margin if all three elements are present; write a question mark if the gambler's fallacy is still embedded in the writing.

framework.learnerExperience: The teacher formally introduces the unit Driving Question: 'If past outcomes of a chance event — like a coin toss or a football match — do not change future probabilities, how can we use mathematics to predict what is likely to happen, and why does this understanding protect us from the dangers of gambling?' The question is displayed prominently (on a poster, whiteboard section, or projected). Learners individually write TWO questions of their own in their exercise books — things they are still wondering about after today's lesson. Selected questions are written on sticky notes (or paper strips) and posted on the class DQB. The DQB is organised into three columns: 'What We Wonder,' 'What We Are Learning,' 'What We Now Know.' Today, all questions go into 'What We Wonder.'
framework.teacherMoves: 1. Read the Driving Question aloud slowly. Ask: 'Which part of this question does today's experiment begin to answer?' WAIT 12 seconds. Take 2 responses. Say: 'Today we answered the first part — past outcomes do NOT change future probability. But we have not yet answered: how do we predict? And how does this protect us from gambling? Those answers will come in the lessons ahead.' 2. Say: 'I want every person to write TWO questions in your book right now. Things you are genuinely curious about after today. You have 2 minutes. They can be about football, betting, dice, cards — anything related to chance.' Start timer. 3. After 2 minutes, ask pairs to share their best question with each other, then select one to write on a paper strip. Collect strips and pin/tape them to the DQB under 'What We Wonder.' Read 5–6 questions aloud to the class. 4. Say: 'Every time we learn something new in this unit, we will move a question from WONDER to LEARNING to KNOW. By the end of this sub-strand, this board will show the journey your thinking has taken.' 5. Take a photo of the DQB (teacher's phone) for documentation. Tell learners: 'This board stays up for the whole unit. Add to it any time you have a new question — even outside class.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Driving Question Board (DQB) Launch. The DQB is a public sensemaking artefact that externalises the class's collective curiosity and tracks growing understanding across the unit. Placing all questions in 'What We Wonder' today creates productive uncertainty — learners know there is more to discover. The physical board (or digital equivalent) makes the learning journey visible and motivates persistence.
framework.formativeAssessment: OBSERVABLE INDICATOR: Every learner has written at least two genuine questions in their exercise book (teacher checks books during the 2-minute writing period). QUALITY INDICATOR: Questions that move beyond 'What is probability?' to questions such as 'Why do betting companies always win in the end?' or 'What happens if you toss a coin 1,000 times?' indicate higher-order thinking. Teacher notes these learners for extension tasks in subsequent lessons.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners create their first individual model (a labelled diagram or annotated sketch) in their exercise books. The model must represent: (a) a coin toss as a system with two equally likely outcomes; (b) the probability value for each outcome (P = 1/2); (c) an arrow or annotation showing that 'past outcomes have NO influence on the next toss' (independence); (d) a connection back to the Gor Mahia scenario — learners draw or write how the coin-toss logic relates (or does NOT relate) to predicting a football match. Models are shared with a partner for a 1-minute peer-review ('What did your partner include that you missed?'), then a revised version is starred in their book as 'Model Version 1.'
framework.teacherMoves: 1. Say: 'Scientists and mathematicians use MODELS to show how a system works. Your model today does not need to be beautiful — it needs to be ACCURATE. Draw a coin. Show the two outcomes. Label the probability of each. Then add an arrow showing what the coin does NOT know.' 2. Demonstrate a partial model on the board (deliberately leave out the independence arrow). Say: 'What is missing from my model?' WAIT 10 seconds. Cold-call one learner. Add the independence annotation based on their suggestion, saying: 'Exactly — I need to show that the coin has NO MEMORY.' 3. Allow 5 minutes for individual model drawing. Circulate and offer targeted prompts: 'Can you show me WHERE in your model the number 0.5 comes from?' / 'How does your model show that tossing heads five times in a row does NOT make tails more likely?' 4. After 5 minutes, run 1-minute peer review. Say: 'Look at your partner's model. Tell them ONE thing they included that is correct and ONE thing they should add or fix. You have 1 minute — go.' 5. Say: 'Put a star next to your model and write: Model Version 1 — [today's date]. We will update this model in every lesson as we learn more. By Lesson 5, your model will show the full picture of probability — including mutually exclusive and independent events.' 6. Close the lesson: 'So — is Gor Mahia due for a loss? What does the mathematics say?' Cold-call one learner for the final word. WAIT 15 seconds. Affirm the correct answer and connect to the DQB: 'That question is now on our board. Let us keep investigating.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Progressive Model Revision (NGSS Science and Engineering Practice: Developing and Using Models). By building an explicit, labelled model on Day 1, learners create a cognitive anchor. The instruction to revisit and revise the model in each subsequent lesson makes conceptual change visible — learners can literally see their own understanding grow. Peer review introduces scientific discourse norms (evidence-based critique) in a low-stakes format.
framework.formativeAssessment: OBSERVABLE INDICATOR: Model Version 1 must contain four elements for 'Meets Expectations': (1) a coin or circle split into two equally labelled sections, (2) P = 1/2 (or 0.5) written for at least one outcome, (3) any annotation conveying 'no memory' / 'independent,' (4) any written or drawn reference to the Gor Mahia/football scenario. Teacher collects exercise books for 5–10 learners at random at the end of the lesson to review models before the next class. Findings are used to plan targeted questioning in Lesson 2.

LESSONS.teacherReflection: After the lesson, reflect on the following questions and write brief notes in your planning diary: (1) MISCONCEPTION TRACKING — How many learners still held the gambler's fallacy in their explanation paragraph (Phase 3)? What specific language did they use? Plan a direct re-address at the opening of Lesson 2 using one of those anonymised examples. (2) DATA QUALITY — Did the pooled class experimental probability fall between 0.45 and 0.55? If it fell outside this range, consider whether coin-tossing technique was inconsistent (spinning rather than flipping). Model correct technique again in Lesson 2. (3) DQB RICHNESS — Were the learners' questions mostly surface-level ('What is probability?') or did any go deeper ('Why do betting companies make money if every event is 50-50?')? The richer questions signal learners who are ready for extension into independent events. (4) MODEL COMPLETENESS — Of the 5–10 books reviewed, how many models included all four required elements? If fewer than 60% included the independence annotation, open Lesson 2 with a whole-class model gallery walk. (5) ENGAGEMENT AND INCLUSION — Were all learners actively tossing and recording, or did some pairs have one dominant partner? In Lesson 2, assign roles explicitly (Tosser, Recorder, Calculator, Reporter) to ensure equitable participation. (6) PCI CONNECTION — Did the gambling/betting discussion remain educational and non-stigmatising? If any learner disclosed personal family experience with gambling, follow up privately and liaise with the school counsellor in line with Life Skills PCI guidance.

summaryTablePrompt.learned: Each coin toss is an independent equally likely event. Theoretical probability = (favourable outcomes) ÷ (total equally likely outcomes). Past outcomes do NOT change future probability — a coin has no memory — directly contradicting the gambler's fallacy promoted in betting advertisements seen on Nairobi matatus and social media.
summaryTablePrompt.explained: The Gor Mahia fan's claim that the team is 'due' for a loss is an example of the gambler's fallacy. Mathematics shows that if each event is independent and equally likely, its probability remains fixed regardless of previous outcomes. Our coin-toss data supported the theoretical P = 0.5, especially when the whole class's results were pooled — showing that larger samples give more reliable estimates of true probability.

slo.purpose: Learners derive and apply the formula P(event) = number of favourable outcomes ÷ total number of equally likely outcomes, using hands-on die-rolling experiments and Kenyan contexts, building the mathematical foundation needed to challenge the gambler's fallacy introduced in the anchoring phenomenon.
slo.knowledge: Learners know that equally likely outcomes are outcomes that have the same chance of occurring; that experimental probability is computed from recorded trials; and that theoretical probability is derived from the formula P(event) = favourable outcomes ÷ total equally likely outcomes.
slo.skills: Learners can perform a die-rolling experiment, record and tally outcomes systematically, compute experimental probabilities as fractions, decimals and percentages, and apply the theoretical probability formula to Kenyan real-life contexts such as drawing a name from a class register or picking a coloured token from a bag.
slo.attitudes: Learners appreciate that mathematics — not intuition, superstition, or betting advertisements — gives us reliable tools for predicting chance events, and develop responsibility in making evidence-based decisions about risk.
slo.keyInquiry: How do we apply probability in day-to-day life?
slo.purposeInStoryline: In Lesson 1, learners explored the anchoring phenomenon — the gambler's fallacy in Gor Mahia FC's winning streak and Nairobi betting culture — and placed their initial questions on the Driving Question Board (DQB). Lesson 2 now gives learners the mathematical tool to begin answering those questions: the probability formula for equally likely outcomes. By rolling a die 60 times and comparing experimental results to theoretical predictions, learners discover that each face always has a 1-in-6 chance regardless of what happened before — directly challenging the 'due for a loss' belief and 'beat the odds' gambling claims from the phenomenon.
slo.safetyNotes: Ensure dice and tokens do not become projectiles; remind learners to roll gently on the desk surface. No sharp objects are used. Githeri-coloured tokens (pebbles, dried beans, or paper squares) are choking hazards — remind learners not to place them in their mouths.

LESSONS.overview: Learners work in groups of five to roll a six-faced die 60 times, tally outcomes, and compute experimental probabilities for each face. Through guided discussion, they derive the theoretical probability formula P(event) = number of favourable outcomes ÷ total number of equally likely outcomes. The teacher then anchors the formula in two Kenyan worked examples: (1) drawing a name from a hat containing 30 learners' names, and (2) picking a coloured token from a bag of githeri-coloured tokens (representing the mixed colours of a githeri serving — white maize, brown beans, green peas). Learners connect their findings back to Gor Mahia FC's winning streak and the betting advertisements, updating the Driving Question Board with new mathematical reasoning. The lesson advances the 8-lesson evidence-gathering sequence by equipping learners with the core formula they will use in all subsequent probability lessons.

framework.learnerExperience: Each group receives a standard six-faced die. Before rolling, learners individually write predictions in their exercise books: (a) If you roll this die 60 times, how many times do you predict each face (1–6) will appear? Record your predicted count for each face. (b) If Gor Mahia FC has won their last 7 matches, does the probability of winning the next match change? Write YES or NO and a one-sentence reason. Learners share predictions with their group partner before the class shares out.
framework.teacherMoves: Distribute one die per group. Say: 'Before we roll a single time, I want each of you — working alone, in silence — to predict how many times each face will appear if we roll 60 times. Write your six predictions in a table in your book. You have 90 seconds.' [Allow 90 seconds of silent individual work.] Then say: 'Now turn to your neighbour and compare predictions. Do you agree? Disagree? Why?' [Allow 60 seconds of pair talk.] Cold-call 3 learners using name sticks: 'Akinyi, what did you predict for face number 6?' — 'Omondi, did you predict the same number for every face, or different numbers? Why?' — 'Fatuma, how did you decide on your number?' [WAIT TIME: 12 seconds after each question before accepting an answer.] Record 3–4 different class predictions on the board without evaluating them. Then say: 'Keep your predictions — at the end of this experiment, we will come back and see who was closest, and more importantly, WHY.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Prediction Anchoring — by committing individual written predictions before the experiment, learners activate prior intuition (often reflecting the gambler's fallacy or vague symmetry thinking). This creates cognitive dissonance when experimental data diverges from prediction, making the theoretical formula more memorable and meaningful.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicator: Every learner has a completed prediction table (6 faces, 6 predicted counts) in their exercise book before rolling begins. Teacher scans the room to confirm all books show written predictions. Listen for prediction reasoning: learners who say 'each face should get 10 because there are 6 faces and 60 rolls' are already reasoning proportionally — note these learners for targeted questioning in the Explain Phase.

framework.learnerExperience: Groups of five roll the die 60 times, with roles assigned: Roller (rolls the die), Caller (calls out the number aloud), Tally Keeper (marks tallies on the group recording sheet), Checker (confirms the tally keeper's mark each time), and Timer/Counter (counts rolls aloud every 10 rolls). After 60 rolls, each learner independently computes the experimental probability for each face as a fraction (e.g., 11/60), a decimal (rounded to 2 d.p.), and a percentage. Groups then compare their experimental probabilities with the teacher-posted class aggregate (teacher compiles all groups' tallies on the board to create a larger combined sample). Learners also observe a short comparison: a bag of githeri-coloured tokens (10 white tokens = maize, 8 brown tokens = beans, 2 green tokens = peas, totalling 20) is passed to each group. Learners predict, then draw one token blindly, record its colour, replace it, and repeat 20 times, recording outcomes.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Your group has a die and a recording sheet. I am going to assign each person a role — listen carefully.' [Assign roles by pointing to each position in the group.] 'The Roller rolls gently on the desk — not on the floor, not in the air. The Caller reads the number loudly so the whole group hears. The Tally Keeper marks the tally. The Checker confirms every single mark. The Timer counts every 10 rolls and announces it. Ready? You have 8 minutes. Begin.' [Circulate to all groups. At the 4-minute mark, announce: 'You should be at approximately 30 rolls by now — check your count.'] After rolling: 'Stop. Now, working individually — not copying your neighbour — compute the experimental probability for each face. Express it as a fraction over 60, then as a decimal to 2 decimal places, then as a percentage. You have 3 minutes.' [Collect one tally from each group. Write the combined class tallies for each face on the board.] Cold-call 2 learners: 'Chebet, what experimental probability did your group get for face number 3? Express it as a fraction.' [WAIT TIME: 10 seconds.] 'Mutua, convert that fraction to a decimal for us.' [WAIT TIME: 12 seconds.] Then introduce the token bag: 'This bag contains tokens in three colours — like the colours in a good githeri: white for maize, brown for beans, green for peas. Before you draw, count the tokens I pour out so you know exactly how many of each colour there are.' [Pour tokens onto a tray, let groups count.] 'Now do 20 draws with replacement. Record each outcome.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Data Aggregation and Pattern Recognition — individual group data (60 rolls) is pooled into a class aggregate (potentially 300–360 rolls across 5–6 groups). This strategy helps learners see that larger sample sizes produce experimental probabilities that converge toward the theoretical value of 1/6 ≈ 0.167, directly modelling the Law of Large Numbers without naming it formally, and setting up the derivation of the theoretical formula.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicators: (1) Each learner's book contains a completed tally table and three rows of probability expressions (fraction, decimal, percentage) for all six faces. (2) During circulation, check that fractions are written with denominator 60 (or the group's total rolls), not simplified incorrectly. (3) Listen for learners who say 'all the fractions are close to 10/60' — these learners are ready for the formula derivation. Red flag: learners writing probabilities greater than 1 or expressing probability as a count rather than a ratio — address immediately with: 'Probability is always a part of a whole — what is the whole here?'

framework.learnerExperience: Using the class aggregate data on the board, learners are guided to articulate the pattern: each face's experimental probability is approximately 1/6. The teacher then introduces the theoretical probability formula: P(event) = number of favourable outcomes ÷ total number of equally likely outcomes. Learners apply the formula to two Kenyan worked examples in their books: (1) Worked Example A — 'Ms Wanjiku writes all 30 learners' names on separate slips of paper and places them in a hat to select one learner to carry the class register to the staffroom. What is the probability that your name is selected?' (2) Worked Example B — 'A bag contains 20 githeri-coloured tokens: 10 white (maize), 8 brown (beans), 2 green (peas). One token is drawn at random. What is the probability of drawing (a) a white token, (b) a brown token, (c) a green token? Do all three probabilities sum to 1? Why?' Learners then return to the Gor Mahia FC phenomenon: 'Using what you now know, explain in one mathematical sentence why Gor Mahia's previous 7 wins do NOT change the probability of the next match result.'
framework.teacherMoves: Point to the class aggregate on the board. Say: 'Look at our combined class data. What do you notice about each face's experimental probability? Discuss with your partner for 30 seconds, then I will ask.' [30 seconds pair talk. Cold-call 2 learners: 'Otieno, what pattern do you see?' WAIT TIME: 12 seconds. 'Njeri, do you agree or disagree with Otieno, and why?' WAIT TIME: 12 seconds.] Then say: 'You have discovered something important. Each face has 1 chance out of 6 equally likely outcomes. That gives us a formula.' [Write on the board in large print:] P(event) = Number of favourable outcomes ÷ Total number of equally likely outcomes. Say: 'Copy this formula into your books and underline it. This is the mathematical engine of probability.' [Pause 30 seconds for copying.] 'Now open to a fresh page. We will do two worked examples together.' [Read Worked Example A aloud. Ask: 'How many favourable outcomes are there for YOUR name being drawn? How many total equally likely outcomes?' WAIT TIME: 10 seconds. Cold-call 1 learner: 'Kamau, give me the fraction.' Confirm: P = 1/30.] [For Worked Example B, say: 'Work this one out individually — parts (a), (b), and (c). Then check whether your three answers sum to 1. You have 3 minutes.' After 3 minutes, cold-call 3 different learners for parts (a), (b), (c). WAIT TIME: 10 seconds each. Then ask: 'Amina, do all three probabilities sum to 1? What does that tell us?' WAIT TIME: 12 seconds.] Finally say: 'Return to Gor Mahia FC. In your book, write ONE mathematical sentence connecting this formula to why their past wins do not change the next match's probability. Use the word equally likely in your sentence. You have 90 seconds.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Formula Derivation from Data (Inductive Reasoning) — rather than presenting the formula as a rule to memorise, the teacher guides learners to extract it from their own experimental data. This inductive path (data → pattern → formula) mirrors NGSS Science and Engineering Practice 4 (Analysing and Interpreting Data) and Practice 6 (Constructing Explanations), ensuring the formula has conceptual roots rather than being an abstract prescription. The Kenyan worked examples (class register, githeri tokens) further ground the formula in familiar, everyday contexts learners trust.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicators: (1) Formula is correctly written and underlined in every learner's book. (2) Worked Example A answer is P = 1/30, correctly labelled. (3) Worked Example B answers are P(white) = 10/20 = 1/2, P(brown) = 8/20 = 2/5, P(green) = 2/20 = 1/10, and learners confirm the sum equals 1 (10/20 + 8/20 + 2/20 = 20/20 = 1). (4) The Gor Mahia sentence explicitly references 'equally likely outcomes' and the formula structure. Red flag: learners writing P = 30/1 (inverted fraction) — address by re-asking 'Which is the part and which is the whole?'

framework.learnerExperience: Each learner writes two sticky-note contributions (or index card entries if sticky notes are unavailable): (1) a CLAIM card — one thing they now know for certain about probability, expressed as a mathematical statement using today's formula; and (2) a QUESTION card — one new question today's lesson raised for them. Groups share their cards, then class representatives pin or tape them to the DQB under two columns: 'What We Now Know' and 'What We Still Wonder'. The teacher draws learners' attention to any DQB questions from Lesson 1 that today's formula has now answered, and physically moves those cards to a 'Solved' section.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Take two cards — one yellow, one blue if available, otherwise just two separate pieces of paper. On the first card, write a CLAIM — something you are now mathematically confident about. Start your sentence with: P(event) = ... On the second card, write a QUESTION — something today raised that you still wonder about. Connect your question to Gor Mahia, the coin toss, or the betting adverts if you can. You have 2 minutes of silent individual writing.' [After 2 minutes: 'Read your claim to your partner. Does your partner agree it is mathematically correct? If not, fix it together.'] [After 60 seconds: 'Bring your cards. Let us update the board.'] [As learners pin cards, read 3 claim cards aloud and confirm or gently correct them. Read 2 question cards aloud and say: 'This is an excellent question — hold onto it. We will have the mathematics to answer it in Lesson 3 or 4.'] Point to Lesson 1 DQB questions about 'what does equally likely mean?' and say: 'Jamil asked in Lesson 1 whether all outcomes must be equally likely for probability to work. Can anyone use today's formula to answer that?' [WAIT TIME: 12 seconds. Cold-call 1 learner.] Move answered cards to the 'Solved' column visibly.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Driving Question Board Curation — the DQB functions as a public, cumulative record of the class's growing understanding. Physically moving Lesson 1 cards to 'Solved' gives learners a visible, tangible sense of intellectual progress. New question cards honour learners' emerging curiosity (e.g., 'What if outcomes are NOT equally likely?' — previewing mutually exclusive and independent events in later lessons) and demonstrate that science and mathematics advance through questions, not just answers.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicators: (1) Every learner produces at least one CLAIM card that correctly uses the formula P(event) = favourable outcomes ÷ total equally likely outcomes with a specific example. (2) QUESTION cards reference the phenomenon (Gor Mahia, coin toss, or betting) rather than being purely abstract. (3) Teacher checks that no claim card contains a probability value greater than 1 or less than 0 — if found, address with the whole class as a teachable moment before the end of the phase.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners return to the probability model they began sketching in Lesson 1 (a simple diagram or written description of what determines the outcome of a chance event). They now add to this model: (1) They annotate their diagram with the formula P(event) = favourable outcomes ÷ total equally likely outcomes, placing it explicitly on the model. (2) They add a new component — a labelled example showing a sample space (all possible outcomes of rolling a die: {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6}) with the favourable outcomes circled. (3) They write one sentence connecting their model to the anchoring phenomenon: 'Each Gor Mahia match result belongs to a sample space of equally likely outcomes; the formula tells us the probability of any single result, and past results do not change the total number of equally likely outcomes in the NEXT match.' Learners share their updated model with a partner and give one piece of feedback using the sentence stem: 'Your model shows ____. One thing to add or change is ____.'
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Get out the model you started in Lesson 1. If you do not have it, redraw the basic structure now — you have 60 seconds.' [Circulate to confirm all learners have a starting model.] 'Now you are going to upgrade your model with three additions. Listen to each one before you draw.' [State addition 1. Pause 45 seconds for learners to annotate.] [State addition 2 — sample space with die faces. Pause 60 seconds.] [State addition 3 — the Gor Mahia sentence. Say: 'This sentence is the heart of what we are building toward. Take your time — 90 seconds.' Pause.] After model work: 'Share your model with your partner. Your partner will tell you one strength and one improvement using the sentence stem on the board.' [Write stem on board: 'Your model shows ____. One thing to add or change is ____.'] [Allow 90 seconds of paired feedback.] Cold-call 2 learners to share their partner's feedback: 'Baraka, what did your partner suggest you add to your model?' [WAIT TIME: 10 seconds.] Close by saying: 'Your models are growing. Each lesson in this sequence, your model will become more powerful — until by Lesson 8 it can explain everything the betting companies and the football commentators get wrong.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Cumulative Model Revision (NGSS Practice 2: Developing and Using Models) — the model is not redrawn from scratch each lesson but iteratively annotated and extended. This mirrors how scientific models evolve with new evidence. Requiring learners to explicitly write the Gor Mahia sentence on their model ensures the abstract formula stays tethered to the anchoring phenomenon and does not become a decontextualised procedure.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicators: (1) Model includes the probability formula correctly stated and labelled. (2) Sample space for a die is listed as {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6} (or equivalent notation) with at least one favourable outcome circled and its probability computed. (3) The Gor Mahia sentence explicitly uses the words 'sample space', 'equally likely', and 'formula' (or 'P(event) ='). (4) Peer feedback is specific (not just 'good job') — teacher circulates and prompts vague feedback: 'Can you point to something specific on the model that shows that?'

LESSONS.teacherReflection: After the lesson, reflect on the following questions in your professional journal: (1) When learners computed experimental probabilities from their die rolls, did the experimental values cluster near 1/6, or were there significant deviations? What does this tell you about the importance of sample size — and how will you address the Law of Large Numbers idea in a future lesson without overwhelming learners now? (2) Did any learner's Gor Mahia sentence on their model reveal persistent gambler's fallacy thinking (e.g., 'past wins make the sample space smaller')? If so, plan a targeted one-on-one conversation before Lesson 3. (3) Were the githeri-coloured token probabilities (1/2, 2/5, 1/10) within reach of all learners, or did some struggle with fractions with different denominators? If fraction fluency is a barrier, consider a brief 5-minute fraction review warm-up at the start of Lesson 3. (4) Review the DQB QUESTION cards: do the learners' new questions naturally lead toward mutually exclusive events (Lesson 3 content)? If so, explicitly reference one of those question cards at the start of Lesson 3 to reinforce the coherent storyline. (5) Was the 40-minute lesson long enough to complete all five phases, including the die-rolling experiment? If time was short, consider having the token-bag observation as a homework extension or a 5-minute starter in Lesson 3.

reading.title: Use Simulations to Explore Experimental Probability (Flexbook)

LESSONS.title: Range of Probability: From Impossible to Certain

slo.purpose: Learners investigate and formalise the boundaries of probability (0 to 1), placing real-life Kenyan events on a probability number line and expressing probability using fractions, decimals, and percentages — building the mathematical foundation needed to dismantle the gambler's fallacy from the anchoring phenomenon.
slo.knowledge: Learners understand that the probability of any event must satisfy 0 ≤ P(event) ≤ 1, where 0 represents an impossible event and 1 represents a certain event; they can express probability as a fraction, decimal, and percentage.
slo.skills: Learners can: (a) determine the range of probability of an event; (b) place events on a probability number line; (c) convert probability expressions between fractions, decimals, and percentages; (d) justify why P > 1 or P < 0 is mathematically impossible.
slo.attitudes: Learners appreciate that probability gives precise, bounded mathematical values to uncertainty, and begin to question culturally promoted misconceptions — such as gambling advertisements on Nairobi matatus claiming one can 'beat the odds' — using this mathematical reasoning.
slo.keyInquiry: How do we apply probability in day-to-day life?
slo.purposeInStoryline: In Lessons 1 and 2 learners established what equally likely events are and computed basic probabilities for coin tosses and dice rolls. In Lesson 3 they now ask: what are the mathematical limits of any probability? By anchoring this in vivid Kenyan scenarios — the certainty of sunrise over Mombasa versus the impossibility of snow in Kisumu in July — learners construct a probability number line (0 to 1) and formalise the range rule. This directly equips them to challenge the gambler's fallacy: if each match is independent and all probabilities are bounded between 0 and 1, no 'streak' can push a future probability outside those bounds. The DQB is updated to reflect this new constraint.
slo.safetyNotes: No physical hazards. Sensitivity note: when discussing gambling advertisements, affirm that no learner or family member is being judged; frame the discussion as mathematical analysis of advertising claims, not personal criticism.

LESSONS.overview: Lesson 3 formalises the range of probability (0 ≤ P ≤ 1) through a structured Predict–Observe–Explain–DQB–Model sequence. Learners first predict where they would place eight Kenyan real-life events on an unmarked line from 'impossible' to 'certain'. They then observe and analyse evidence — a short Kenyan scenario card set and a class coin-toss frequency table accumulated in Lesson 1 — to test their predictions. In the Explain phase, learners formalise that no experiment can yield P > 1 or P < 0, convert between fraction, decimal, and percentage representations, and connect this directly back to Gor Mahia's winning streak: no matter how long the streak, the probability of winning or losing the next match remains bounded between 0 and 1, never becoming 'inevitable'. Learners update the Driving Question Board and revise their cumulative probability model to include the 0-to-1 constraint boundary.

framework.learnerExperience: Each learner receives a strip of paper representing a blank number line labelled 'Impossible' at the left end and 'Certain' at the right end. They are given a set of eight Event Cards (printed or read aloud) describing Kenyan scenarios, e.g.: (1) The sun rises tomorrow over Mombasa. (2) It snows in Kisumu in July. (3) A flipped 10-shilling coin lands on heads. (4) Gor Mahia wins their very next Premier League match. (5) A matatu from Nairobi to Nakuru takes exactly 2 hours with no traffic. (6) A student chosen at random from a class of 40 is a girl, if 20 are girls. (7) A ripe mango falls upward when dropped. (8) It rains at least once in Nairobi in April. Learners individually place each event on their number line using a letter code (A–H), then write a one-sentence justification for each placement. They do NOT yet assign numerical values.
framework.teacherMoves: Distribute Event Cards and blank number line strips. Say: 'Before we do any mathematics today, I want to see what your instincts tell you. Place each event somewhere on this line — do not worry about exact numbers yet. You have 5 minutes, working alone.' Allow 5 minutes of silent individual work. After 5 minutes, say: 'Turn to your neighbour and compare your placements. Do you agree? If not, try to convince each other using one reason.' Allow 3 minutes of pair discussion. Cold-call 4 learners (choose one confident, one hesitant, one who seems to have placed an event differently from peers, and one who has written a detailed justification): 'Tell me where you placed Event 2 — snow in Kisumu — and why.' After each response, wait 12 seconds before probing: 'Does anyone place this differently? Why?' Do NOT confirm or correct yet. Record the class's most common placements on the board using tally marks next to each event label to create visible disagreement.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Elicitation of prior knowledge via anchored prediction: by forcing placements on a physical continuum before instruction, learners activate intuitive understanding of likelihood. Recording disagreements publicly creates cognitive dissonance that motivates the Observe phase. Connecting events to vivid Kenyan contexts (Kisumu snow, Nairobi April rain, Gor Mahia match) makes the abstraction of 'range' personally meaningful.
framework.formativeAssessment: Circulate during individual work. Look for: (a) learners who place 'impossible' and 'certain' events in the middle of the line — flag for targeted questioning in Phase 3; (b) learners who correctly distinguish near-certain (Nairobi rain in April) from certain (sunrise) — note as potential peer explainers. Collect 4–5 strips at random to review justifications before the Explain phase.

framework.learnerExperience: Activity A — Scenario Card Analysis (15 min): In groups of 4, learners receive a set of 6 'Evidence Cards'. Each card presents a Kenyan scenario with a completed sample space, e.g.: Card 1 — 'A bag contains 3 red and 3 blue maize kernels. One is picked at random.' Sample space = {R, R, R, B, B, B}. Favourable outcomes for 'picking red' = 3. Total outcomes = 6. Learners are asked to write the probability as a fraction, then convert it to a decimal and a percentage. Card 2 — 'A student randomly picks one fruit from a bowl containing only mangoes. What is the probability of picking a mango?' Card 3 — 'A student randomly picks one fruit from a bowl containing only mangoes. What is the probability of picking a guava?' Cards 4–6 escalate: a six-faced die, a football match with 3 outcomes (win/draw/lose), and a spinner divided into 5 equal sections. For each card, learners record: fraction, decimal, percentage, and position on their number line. Activity B — Accumulated Coin-Toss Data (5 min): The teacher displays the class's running coin-toss frequency table built in Lesson 1 (total tosses ≈ 200+ across the class). Learners calculate the experimental probability of heads as a fraction, decimal, and percentage, then compare to the theoretical value of 0.5.
framework.teacherMoves: Distribute Evidence Cards to each group. Say: 'Your job is to be mathematical detectives. For each card, calculate the probability, then write it three ways: as a fraction, as a decimal, and as a percentage. Then place it on your number line. You have 12 minutes.' Set a visible timer. Circulate — do NOT give answers. Use prompt questions: 'How many outcomes are in the sample space?' (wait 10 seconds), 'How many of those are favourable?' (wait 10 seconds), 'What does it mean if the number of favourable outcomes equals zero?' (wait 15 seconds — this targets Cards 2 and 3 for impossible/certain recognition). After 12 minutes, call the class back. Display the accumulated coin-toss data on the board. Ask: 'Look at our data from the last two lessons. What is the experimental probability of heads as a decimal? As a percentage?' Cold-call 2 learners. Then ask: 'Is this value closer to 0 or to 1, or somewhere in between?' (wait 12 seconds). Ask: 'Did any group get a probability fraction where the numerator was larger than the denominator?' (pause 10 seconds). 'What would that even mean?'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Concrete-to-abstract bridging using graduated Evidence Cards: Cards begin with physically tangible Kenyan objects (maize kernels, fruit bowls) before moving to abstract spinners, so all learners access the mathematics. The impossible and certain cards (only mangoes, picking guava) create the 0 and 1 anchor points experientially before they are formalised. Connecting to the class's own accumulated coin-toss data from Lesson 1 reinforces continuity of evidence across the storyline.
framework.formativeAssessment: Walk the room during group work. Observable indicators of understanding: (a) learners correctly write P = 0 for the 'impossible' card and P = 1 for the 'certain' card; (b) learners successfully convert fractions to decimals and percentages without prompting; (c) learners place all six events between or at 0 and 1 on the number line. Observable indicators of confusion: (d) learners write P = 6/6 = 1 but do not connect this to 'certain'; (e) learners cannot convert fractions to decimals — note for targeted support in Explain phase. Check at least 3 groups' written work before transitioning.

framework.learnerExperience: Part A — Formalising the Number Line (10 min): Each learner now draws a formal probability number line in their exercise books, labelling 0 (Impossible) and 1 (Certain), and marking 0.5 (½, 50%) at the midpoint. They revisit their Event Cards from Phase 1 and now assign numerical values (fractions, decimals, percentages) to each event, correcting their original placements where needed. They write a formal probability statement for at least 4 of the 8 events, e.g., 'P(sun rises over Mombasa tomorrow) = 1' and 'P(snow in Kisumu in July) = 0'. Part B — The Impossibility of P > 1 and P < 0 (8 min): Learners read a short 2-paragraph printed or on-screen text: a fictional betting advertisement claiming 'Our algorithm gives you a 120% chance of predicting the winner!' Learners are asked: 'What is mathematically wrong with this claim? Use what you know about the range of probability to explain in two sentences.' They write their response individually, then share with a partner. Part C — Connecting to the Phenomenon (5 min): The teacher returns to the Gor Mahia phenomenon. Learners answer in their books: 'A sports commentator says after Gor Mahia's 8th consecutive win: the probability of them winning the next match has now risen above 1 because they are on such a hot streak. Using the range of probability, explain why this commentator is mathematically wrong.'
framework.teacherMoves: Open Part A by saying: 'Now we are going to make your intuitions precise. Open your books to a fresh page. Draw a line — label the left end 0 and write Impossible, label the right end 1 and write Certain. Mark 0.5 in the middle.' Give learners 2 minutes to draw and label. Then say: 'Go back to your Event Cards. This time, I want a number — not just a position. Write P(event) = [fraction] = [decimal] = [percentage] for at least four events.' Allow 5 minutes. Cold-call 3 learners to share one event each — choose deliberately: one certain, one impossible, one middle-ground. After each, ask the class: 'Agree or disagree? Thumbs up or down. Why?' Wait 10 seconds after each thumb response before elaborating. For Part B, distribute or display the fictional advertisement. Say: 'A company is advertising gambling odds. Read this carefully. What is wrong — mathematically wrong — with their claim? You have 3 minutes to write your answer alone.' After 3 minutes: 'Share with your partner. Decide on the best one-sentence mathematical argument between you.' Cold-call 2 pairs. After responses, say firmly: 'Probability can never exceed 1. It can never be less than 0. This is not an opinion — it is a mathematical law. If anyone ever shows you odds above 100%, they are either making a mistake or deliberately misleading you.' For Part C, say: 'Now apply this directly to Gor Mahia. Write your answer in your book. Two sentences minimum.' Allow 4 minutes. Cold-call 2 learners. Conclude: 'No winning streak — not Gor Mahia's, not anyone's — can push the probability of the next event above 1 or below 0. The mathematics does not allow it.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Three-part explain sequence using claim-evidence-reasoning (CER): learners first build the formal number line (claim), then use the betting advertisement to construct a refutation (evidence + reasoning), then apply reasoning directly to the phenomenon (transfer). The CER structure is an NGSS Science and Engineering Practice (Constructing Explanations) applied to mathematics. Returning to the phenomenon in Part C ensures every phase of the lesson ties back to the storyline and driving question.
framework.formativeAssessment: Collect exercise books from 6 learners (2 high, 2 middle, 2 struggling based on prior lessons) at the end of Part A to check: (a) correct numerical values assigned to certain and impossible events; (b) correct fraction-decimal-percentage conversions. During Part B, listen for the key phrase 'probability cannot exceed 1' or equivalent — if fewer than half the class produces this in their written responses, pause and reteach using the maize kernel example before proceeding to Part C. In Part C, the written response about Gor Mahia serves as an exit check for the core SLO: learners must reference 0 ≤ P ≤ 1 explicitly.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners return to the class Driving Question Board. They individually write one sticky note (or a slip of paper) responding to the prompt: 'What does today's lesson add to our answer to the driving question: If past outcomes do not change future probabilities, how can mathematics protect us from gambling?' They must reference the range of probability (0 to 1) in their response. Learners also scan the existing DQB cards from Lessons 1 and 2 and identify one question that today's lesson has now partially or fully answered. They mark it with a tick and write a brief explanation on the reverse side. A class scribe (rotating role) reads out 3–4 new sticky notes and the class votes (show of hands) on which one best advances the driving question.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Look at our Driving Question Board. We have been building an answer across three lessons. Today's piece is about limits — mathematical boundaries. On your sticky note, explain how knowing that probability must stay between 0 and 1 helps us respond to the driving question. You have 3 minutes.' After writing, say: 'Now scan the board. Find one question from Lesson 1 or 2 that you can now answer — or partially answer — because of what you learned today. Mark it and write your answer on the back. 2 minutes.' Call the class scribe to read out 3–4 new notes. After each, ask: 'Does this advance our driving question? Thumbs up or sideways.' After voting, say: 'Pin the strongest ones near the top of the board — they are moving us closer to the answer.' End by framing the next lesson: 'We now know probabilities are bounded. In Lesson 4, we ask: what happens when two events cannot both occur at the same time — like Gor Mahia both winning and losing the same match?'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Progressive DQB construction as a visible thinking routine: by physically marking previously posted questions as 'answered', learners see their own growing understanding made tangible. The voting mechanism creates collaborative epistemic accountability — the class, not just the teacher, evaluates the quality of reasoning. Connecting the DQB update to the phenomenon and previewing Lesson 4 maintains storyline coherence.
framework.formativeAssessment: Read all sticky notes after class. Look for: (a) learners who correctly cite '0 ≤ P ≤ 1' as the constraint — these learners have met the SLO; (b) learners who write only vague statements like 'probability is between 0 and 1' without connecting to gambling or the phenomenon — provide written feedback prompting them to make the connection explicit; (c) learners who cannot identify any previously answered question — flag for individual check-in at the start of Lesson 4.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners open their cumulative probability model (begun in Lesson 1 as a hand-drawn or digital diagram). In Lesson 1 they added equally likely events and sample spaces; in Lesson 2 they added the probability formula P = favourable outcomes / total outcomes. Today they add a new layer: a clearly drawn and labelled probability number line (0 to 1) with at least four Kenyan events placed on it. They annotate the model with: (a) a boundary rule box stating '0 ≤ P(any event) ≤ 1 — this is always true'; (b) an arrow pointing from the Gor Mahia winning streak scenario to the number line with the annotation 'no streak changes the boundaries'; (c) a colour-coded legend distinguishing impossible (red, P=0), certain (green, P=1), and intermediate (blue, 0 < P < 1) events. Learners share their updated model with a shoulder partner for 2 minutes of peer feedback, using the prompt: 'Is the number line correctly labelled? Are the Kenyan events placed accurately? Is the boundary rule written clearly?'
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Take out your cumulative probability model. We are adding today's learning to it. Your model should now show three things we have learned across three lessons: sample spaces, the probability formula, and now the range. You have 8 minutes to update it.' Circulate — do NOT draw the model for any learner, but use targeted questions: 'Where does P = 0 sit on your number line?' (wait 10 seconds); 'Can you find a Kenyan event to place at exactly 0.5?' (wait 12 seconds); 'What does your annotation say about Gor Mahia's streak?' (wait 10 seconds). After 8 minutes: 'Share with your shoulder partner. Use the three-question peer feedback prompt on the board. You have 2 minutes.' After peer feedback: 'Make any corrections. Your model is a living document — it will grow every lesson.' Conclude the lesson by saying: 'Three lessons in, we have built a foundation: probability is a number bounded between 0 and 1. No superstition, no streak, no betting algorithm can change that mathematical fact. Hold onto that as we continue.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Cumulative model revision as an NGSS Developing and Using Models practice: each lesson's model update forces learners to integrate new knowledge with prior knowledge rather than treating each lesson as isolated. The colour-coding system creates a visual schema that persists across all 8 lessons. Peer feedback using a structured 3-question prompt builds metacognitive awareness and communication competency as mandated by KICD core competencies.
framework.formativeAssessment: Conduct a gallery walk of 6–8 models (quickly) while learners do peer feedback. Look for: (a) probability number line correctly anchored at 0 and 1 with accurate event placements — this is the core SLO indicator; (b) the boundary rule written in the learner's own words (not copied verbatim) — indicates genuine understanding; (c) the Gor Mahia annotation connecting the phenomenon to the range rule — indicates storyline transfer. Any model missing the boundary rule annotation should receive a written question: 'What happens to P if the numerator of your fraction is larger than the denominator? Can that ever happen?' to prompt self-correction before Lesson 4.

LESSONS.teacherReflection: After the lesson, reflect on the following questions: (1) Did learners successfully distinguish between 'near-certain' events (e.g., rain in Nairobi in April) and 'certain' events (e.g., sunrise over Mombasa) — if not, what Kenyan examples would make this distinction sharper in Lesson 4's review? (2) During Part B of the Explain phase, how many learners independently used the language '0 ≤ P ≤ 1' without being prompted — if fewer than 60%, consider opening Lesson 4 with a 5-minute retrieval warm-up using two more betting-advertisement claims to reactivate the boundary rule. (3) Were there learners who struggled with the fraction-to-decimal-to-percentage conversion? If so, note their names and plan a brief bridging task at the start of Lesson 4 using familiar Kenyan currency (e.g., 50 cents out of 1 shilling = 0.5 = 50%) to scaffold the conversion before the lesson proceeds to mutually exclusive events. (4) Did the DQB sticky notes show genuine engagement with the gambling/phenomenon connection, or were they procedural restatements of the rule? If the latter, consider adding a 'so what?' sentence-starter prompt ('This matters for our driving question because…') to the DQB protocol in Lesson 4. (5) How is the cumulative model developing across the class — are learners treating it as a meaningful record of growing understanding, or as a task to complete? If the latter, consider projecting one strong model anonymously at the start of Lesson 4 and discussing what makes it a good thinking tool.

summaryTablePrompt.observed: Learners analysed Kenyan scenario Evidence Cards (maize kernels, fruit bowls, dice, spinners) and the class's accumulated coin-toss data from Lesson 1 to find probabilities and place them on a number line.
summaryTablePrompt.learned: The probability of any event must satisfy 0 ≤ P(event) ≤ 1; P = 0 means impossible (e.g., snow in Kisumu in July); P = 1 means certain (e.g., sunrise over Mombasa); all other events fall strictly between 0 and 1, and no winning streak — including Gor Mahia's — can push a future probability outside these bounds.
summaryTablePrompt.explained: Learners used the range of probability to refute a fictional gambling advertisement claiming '120% odds', and wrote a mathematical explanation of why a sports commentator claiming Gor Mahia's winning streak raises their probability above 1 is mathematically impossible, using the boundary rule 0 ≤ P ≤ 1.
