LESSONS.title: Mutually Exclusive Events — Identification & The Addition Rule

slo.purpose: Learners will identify mutually exclusive events in real-life Kenyan contexts and calculate the probability of mutually exclusive events using the addition rule P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B), connecting this understanding to the anchoring phenomenon of the Gambler's Fallacy and the dangers of gambling.
slo.knowledge: Learners will know that: (a) mutually exclusive events are events that cannot occur at the same time; (b) for mutually exclusive events, P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B); (c) the addition rule applies only when events share no outcomes (P(A and B) = 0); (d) many gambling predictions falsely treat non-mutually-exclusive outcomes as certain, exploiting misunderstanding of the addition rule.
slo.skills: Learners will be able to: (a) identify whether two events are mutually exclusive or not from a description or experiment; (b) sort a set of events into 'mutually exclusive' and 'not mutually exclusive' categories with justification; (c) calculate P(A or B) using the addition rule for mutually exclusive events from single-chance experiments (one die, one card draw, one raffle draw); (d) explain why the addition rule cannot be blindly applied to non-mutually-exclusive events.
slo.attitudes: Learners will appreciate that: (a) precise mathematical language prevents costly errors — including in gambling decisions; (b) working collaboratively to sort and justify event classifications builds shared mathematical understanding; (c) probability mathematics protects communities from exploitation by gambling advertisers who blur distinctions between mutually exclusive outcomes.
slo.keyInquiry: How do we apply probability in day-to-day life?
slo.purposeInStoryline: In Lessons 1–3, learners established equally likely events, the probability range [0,1], and the independence of each match or coin toss from past results. Lesson 4 now asks: when we combine outcomes — 'What is the probability that Gor Mahia wins OR draws this match?' — how do we add probabilities correctly? Learners discover that the addition rule only works cleanly when the two outcomes cannot both happen at once (mutually exclusive). This directly addresses gambling ads on Nairobi matatus that imply bettors can simply 'add up' their chances across multiple simultaneous selections — a mathematically flawed shortcut that costs bettors money.
slo.safetyNotes: No physical hazards. Sensitivity note: some learners may have family members affected by gambling addiction. The teacher should frame all gambling-related discussions around mathematical literacy and protection, never judgment of individuals. Use 'gambling advertisements exploit misunderstanding of probability' framing, not 'gamblers are foolish.'

LESSONS.overview: Learners open by revisiting the Gor Mahia / betting-advertisement phenomenon and are challenged with a new question: 'If a bettor picks Gor Mahia to win AND to draw the same match, can those both happen? What is the probability of one OR the other?' Through a card-sorting activity using Kenyan context event cards, learners classify events as mutually exclusive or not. They then conduct a structured die-rolling and raffle-simulation experiment to verify the addition rule P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) for mutually exclusive events. Guided examples anchor the rule to the school raffle and football match scenarios. Learners update their Driving Question Board and revise their cumulative probability model.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners are shown a slide/board prompt: 'A sports betting slip shows two selections for a SINGLE Gor Mahia match: (A) Gor Mahia WINS, (B) Gor Mahia DRAWS. The advertiser says: your chance of being right is P(Win) + P(Draw) = 1/3 + 1/3 = 2/3. Is this claim correct? Can both A and B happen on the same match? Write your prediction and reason in your exercise book — do NOT discuss yet.' Learners write individually for 3 minutes, then share with a shoulder partner for 2 minutes.
framework.teacherMoves: Display the prompt on the board or ARES screen. Say: 'Before we investigate anything today, I want your honest prediction. There is no wrong answer yet — I want to see your thinking.' Give WAIT TIME of 3 minutes of silent writing. Circulate and note 3–4 different responses (one who says 'yes, add them,' one who says 'no, they can't both happen,' one who is unsure). After partner share, cold-call exactly 3 learners: 'Amina, what did you predict and why?' / 'Ochieng, do you agree or disagree with Amina?' / 'Wanjiru, what did your partner say that surprised you?' Record key prediction phrases verbatim on the board under the heading 'OUR PREDICTIONS — we will test these today.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Elicit-and-Record: capturing raw predictions publicly creates cognitive dissonance when evidence later contradicts them, motivating genuine inquiry. Connecting to the betting-advertisement phenomenon ensures learners see immediate real-world relevance.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicator: every learner has a written prediction with a reason in their book before discussion begins. Teacher scans books during circulation — look for whether learners use the word 'same match' or 'at the same time' as a natural constraint; this reveals prior intuition about mutual exclusivity. Note which learners conflate 'adding probabilities' with 'combining events' — these learners need targeted questioning in Phase 3.

framework.learnerExperience: ACTIVITY A — Event Card Sort (15 min): Each group of 4 receives a set of 10 event-cards (printed or written on cut paper). Each card describes two events for the SAME single trial. Groups physically sort cards into two piles: 'CAN happen at the same time' and 'CANNOT happen at the same time.' Event cards include: (1) Rolling a die: getting a 3 AND getting a 5; (2) Rolling a die: getting an even number AND getting a number greater than 4; (3) Drawing one card: drawing a Heart AND drawing a Spade; (4) Drawing one card: drawing a King AND drawing a Heart; (5) A matatu from Nairobi CBD: arriving in Mombasa AND arriving in Kisumu at the same time; (6) A learner's Grade 10 exam result: scoring an A AND scoring a D on the same paper; (7) Gor Mahia's match result: winning AND drawing the same match; (8) Picking one ball from a bag of red, blue and green balls: picking red AND picking blue; (9) Picking one ball: picking red AND picking a ball that is NOT green; (10) A raffle ticket: winning 1st prize AND winning 2nd prize in a raffle where one ticket wins one prize only. Groups record their sorted lists and write a one-sentence justification for each. ACTIVITY B — Die-Roll Experiment (10 min): Each pair rolls a standard die 30 times. They record: frequency of rolling a 2 (Event A), frequency of rolling a 5 (Event B), frequency of rolling a 2 OR a 5 (Event A or B). They compute experimental probabilities. Class results are pooled on the board into a tally table.
framework.teacherMoves: Distribute event cards to groups. Say: 'Your job is simple — for each card, ask: on ONE single trial, can BOTH things happen at exactly the same time? If yes, one pile. If no, other pile. Do not use any vocabulary I have taught you yet — use your own words.' Give groups 10 minutes. Circulate and listen — do NOT correct yet. Note groups who correctly identify card (4) King AND Heart as 'CAN happen' — this is the key diagnostic. After sorting, say: 'Keep your piles. We will come back to them.' Transition to die-rolling: 'Now let us collect actual data.' Distribute dice. Say: 'Roll 30 times. Each time, record what you got. We want to know: how often do you get a 2? How often a 5? How often either a 2 or a 5?' After 10 minutes, call table representatives to report frequencies. Record class totals on the board. Calculate class-level experimental P(2) ≈ 1/6, P(5) ≈ 1/6, P(2 or 5) ≈ 2/6. Give WAIT TIME of 15 seconds after writing the three values and ask: 'What pattern do you notice about these three numbers?' Cold-call 2 learners before explaining.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Concrete Manipulation + Data Collection: the physical card sort activates embodied reasoning about simultaneity before formal vocabulary is introduced. The die experiment provides empirical evidence that P(A or B) ≈ P(A) + P(B) for these events, making the later algebraic rule feel discovered rather than imposed. Pooling class data reduces sampling error and models scientific practice.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicator 1: each group's card-sort correctly places cards (1), (3), (5), (6), (7), (8), (10) in 'CANNOT happen' and cards (2), (4), (9) in 'CAN happen.' Card (4) — King AND Heart — is the key diagnostic: groups who place it in 'CANNOT happen' reveal a misconception that different categories are always mutually exclusive; flag these groups for targeted questioning in Phase 3. Observable indicator 2: in the die experiment, learners record P(2 or 5) as a value close to but not equal to P(2) + P(5) due to sampling variation — check that learners interpret this as 'close to' not 'exactly,' building realistic data-literacy expectations.

framework.learnerExperience: STEP 1 — Vocabulary Anchoring (5 min): Teacher introduces the formal term 'mutually exclusive events' and links it directly to learners' own card-sort language. Learners re-label their two piles using the new term. STEP 2 — Addition Rule Derivation (10 min): Teacher works through three guided examples on the board, using the school-raffle and football-match contexts. Example 1 (raffle): 'A school raffle at Nakuru High School has 50 tickets. Mwangi holds ticket 7. Event A = Mwangi wins 1st prize (one winner). Event B = Mwangi wins 2nd prize (one winner, different ticket). Are A and B mutually exclusive? P(A) = 1/50. P(B) = 1/50. P(A or B) = ?' Learners calculate individually, then teacher confirms P(A or B) = 2/50 = 1/25. Example 2 (die): 'Roll one die. P(rolling a 2 or a 5) = ?' Links to their experimental data. Example 3 (non-mutually exclusive, contrast): 'Draw one card from a standard deck. Event A = King. Event B = Heart. Are these mutually exclusive?' — Teacher deliberately returns to card (4) from the sort. Learners debate: 'Can a card be BOTH a King AND a Heart? Yes — King of Hearts exists!' Therefore P(A or B) ≠ P(A) + P(B). Teacher states: 'Today we only apply the addition rule when events ARE mutually exclusive.' STEP 3 — Gambling Advertisement Deconstruction (8 min): Teacher displays a mock betting-slip advertisement (Nairobi matatu style): 'Pick Gor Mahia to WIN or DRAW — 2 chances out of 3! Your odds are great!' Learners work in pairs: 'Is WIN and DRAW mutually exclusive for ONE match? So can we use P(Win or Draw) = P(Win) + P(Draw)? What does this actually equal if each outcome has probability 1/3?' Learners calculate P(Win or Draw) = 2/3. Teacher asks: 'So is the advertiser's maths correct here? Why might the advertiser WANT you to focus on this number instead of P(Lose) = 1/3?' Learners discuss the psychological and mathematical manipulation.
framework.teacherMoves: For Step 1, point to the 'CANNOT happen at the same time' pile and say: 'Mathematicians have a precise name for exactly what you described — events that CANNOT occur simultaneously on a single trial are called MUTUALLY EXCLUSIVE events. Write this definition in your own words beneath the one I will write.' Write on board: 'Two events are mutually exclusive if they cannot both occur in a single trial. P(A and B) = 0.' Give WAIT TIME of 15 seconds. For Step 2, after writing Example 1, say: 'Do not watch me — calculate P(A or B) yourself first. 30 seconds.' Cold-call 1 learner for the answer. Then ask: 'How did the addition rule appear in your die experiment from Activity B? Did it hold exactly?' Cold-call 2 learners. For Step 3 (gambling deconstruction), say: 'Work with your partner. I want two things: first, confirm whether WIN and DRAW are mutually exclusive for one match. Second, tell me whether the advertiser's claim is mathematically correct AND whether 2/3 is the full picture.' After 3 minutes, cold-call 3 pairs. Conclude by saying: 'The advertiser is technically correct about the addition — but they are hiding P(Lose) = 1/3 and they are ignoring that across MANY bets, independent losses accumulate. This is what Lessons 1–3 showed us about independence.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Bridging from Concrete to Formal: the explicit connection from learners' own card-sort language to the formal definition creates ownership of the vocabulary. The contrast case (King AND Heart) is essential — without a non-mutually-exclusive example, learners over-generalise the addition rule. The gambling advertisement deconstruction uses the 'Claim-Evidence-Reasoning' framework: learners identify the claim, test it with their probability tools, and reason about the advertiser's intent.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicator 1: during Example 3, all learners should be able to name the King of Hearts as the counter-example that makes WIN a King AND a Heart non-mutually exclusive — scan the room for written notes confirming this. Observable indicator 2: during the gambling deconstruction, listen for learners who can spontaneously connect back to Lesson 3 (independence) — these learners are demonstrating cross-lesson integration. Red flag: any learner who says 'P(Win or Draw) = 2/3 means you'll win 2 out of every 3 bets' is conflating probability with certainty — address immediately with: 'Does probability tell us what WILL happen, or what is LIKELY over many trials?'

framework.learnerExperience: Each learner reviews the class Driving Question Board (established in Lesson 1): 'If past outcomes of a chance event do not change future probabilities, how can we use mathematics to predict what is likely to happen, and why does this understanding protect us from the dangers of gambling?' Learners individually write on a sticky note or in their ARES journal: (a) ONE new understanding from today that advances the driving question — e.g., 'I can now calculate the probability of Gor Mahia winning OR drawing using the addition rule, but only because those outcomes can't happen simultaneously'; (b) ONE new question the day's learning raised — e.g., 'What happens to the addition rule when events CAN overlap, like drawing a King or a Heart?' The class adds new question-notes to the DQB under the heading 'Mutually Exclusive Events.' The teacher reads 3–4 notes aloud and connects them to the lesson sequence: 'Notice how Lesson 3 told us independence means past results don't matter. Today's lesson tells us that when outcomes are mutually exclusive, we can ADD their probabilities for a single trial. These are two different tools.'
framework.teacherMoves: Distribute sticky notes or direct learners to the DQB journal page. Say: 'You have 4 minutes. Two things only: one thing you now understand better about our driving question, and one new question today's lesson raised for you.' After 4 minutes, cold-call 3 learners to share their new questions. Write the new questions on the DQB physically or on the ARES platform board. Point to the existing DQB entries from Lessons 1–3 and say: 'Look at the question from Lesson 2 about whether we can predict a coin landing on heads. How does today's lesson — about adding mutually exclusive probabilities — connect to that earlier question?' Give WAIT TIME of 15 seconds. Cold-call 2 learners. Affirm and clarify: 'Each lesson is giving us one more mathematical tool. The driving question asks us to use ALL of them together.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Metacognitive Monitoring via DQB: the Driving Question Board functions as a public, cumulative record of the class's growing understanding. By requiring both an 'understanding gained' and a 'new question raised,' the protocol reinforces that science and mathematics are iterative — new knowledge always generates new questions. Connecting current DQB entries to prior-lesson entries builds the narrative arc of the 8-lesson sequence.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicator: learners' 'understanding' statements should reference at minimum ONE of the following: (a) the definition of mutually exclusive events, (b) the addition rule, or (c) a Kenyan-context example from today. Learners whose statements are vague ('I learned about probability') need a follow-up prompt: 'Can you name a specific example from today that showed you this?' New questions appearing on the DQB that anticipate future lessons (e.g., about overlapping events, or about multiple bets) indicate learners who are ready for extension.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners retrieve their cumulative probability model from Lesson 3 (a diagram or annotated framework showing: equally likely events, probability range [0,1], independence of events across trials). They now ADD a new layer to the model specifically for a single trial: a branching diagram showing one die roll with all six outcomes. They annotate: (a) circle or bracket events that ARE mutually exclusive (e.g., {rolling a 2} and {rolling a 5}); (b) write P(2 or 5) = P(2) + P(5) = 1/6 + 1/6 = 2/6 = 1/3 alongside; (c) annotate the Gor Mahia match branch: outcomes WIN / DRAW / LOSE — all three are mutually exclusive for one match, so P(Win or Draw) = 1/3 + 1/3 = 2/3; (d) add a RED WARNING BOX: 'Addition rule for mutually exclusive events ONLY — does NOT apply when outcomes can overlap (e.g., King AND Heart).' Learners share their updated model with a partner and explain one annotation aloud before the lesson ends.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Take out your probability model from Lesson 3. Today you are adding a new layer — the addition rule for mutually exclusive events on a SINGLE trial. This is separate from what we learned about independence, which was about MULTIPLE trials over time.' Give learners 8 minutes to annotate. Circulate and check that: (1) the branching die diagram clearly shows all six outcomes labelled; (2) mutually exclusive event pairs are visually bracketed or circled; (3) the addition rule is written as a formula, not just a number; (4) the RED WARNING BOX about non-mutually-exclusive events is present. After 8 minutes, say: 'Turn to your partner. Point to ONE part of your model and explain it out loud using the words: mutually exclusive, addition rule, and single trial. You have 2 minutes.' Cold-call 2 pairs to share. Close by connecting to the phenomenon: 'When the betting advertisement on the matatu says Gor Mahia will WIN or DRAW — they are using the addition rule correctly for one match. But as we proved in Lesson 3, knowing the probability of one match tells you nothing about whether they will win the NEXT one. That is the gambler's fallacy — and it is how betting companies make their money.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Cumulative Model Revision: requiring learners to physically annotate an ongoing model — rather than redraw it each lesson — makes conceptual growth visible and tangible. The RED WARNING BOX is a deliberate metacognitive device: it forces learners to encode the boundary condition of the rule, preventing over-generalisation. The partner explanation (verbal model) reinforces encoding through the dual-coding of visual and linguistic representation.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicator 1: the completed model diagram includes all four required components (branching diagram, mutually exclusive brackets, addition rule formula, red warning box). Use this as a 2-minute observation checklist while circulating. Observable indicator 2: during partner explanation, listen for correct use of the phrase 'single trial' — learners who omit this qualifier may be conflating the addition rule with multi-trial calculations. Observable indicator 3: the red warning box demonstrates awareness of the rule's boundary condition — learners who include a specific example (King of Hearts) in the box show deeper understanding than those who write only a general statement.

LESSONS.teacherReflection: After the lesson, reflect on the following: (1) CARD SORT DIAGNOSTIC — Did most groups correctly identify card (4) — King AND Heart — as NOT mutually exclusive? If groups placed it in the 'CANNOT happen' pile, the next lesson must revisit overlapping events before proceeding to independent events. Note the proportion of groups who got this right without prompting. (2) ADDITION RULE OWNERSHIP — During the guided examples, did learners calculate P(A or B) before you showed them, or did they wait to copy? If learners waited, consider restructuring Phase 3 next time to require written individual working before any class discussion. (3) GAMBLING DECONSTRUCTION — Did the Gor Mahia advertisement discussion remain focused on mathematical critique, or did it drift into general opinions about gambling? If it drifted, prepare a tighter prompt for Lesson 5: 'We are mathematicians analysing claims, not judges of people's choices.' (4) DQB QUALITY — Review the sticky notes added to the DQB. Are learners' new questions getting more mathematically sophisticated across lessons (from 'what is probability?' in Lesson 1 to 'what about overlapping events?' in Lesson 4)? If questions are not advancing, the learners may not be reading prior DQB entries — build in a 2-minute silent DQB review at the start of Lesson 5. (5) MODEL COHERENCE — Do learners' updated models clearly separate the concept of independence (across multiple trials, first met informally in Lesson 1) from mutual exclusivity (within a single trial, introduced today)? Confusion between these two concepts is the most common error at this point in the sub-strand and must be resolved before Lesson 5.

summaryTablePrompt.observed: Learners sorted 10 Kenyan-context event-cards into 'mutually exclusive' and 'not mutually exclusive' piles, justifying each placement. They also rolled a die 30 times each and recorded experimental frequencies for Event A (rolling a 2), Event B (rolling a 5), and Event A or B (rolling a 2 or a 5), pooling class data on the board.
summaryTablePrompt.learned: Mutually exclusive events are events that cannot occur simultaneously on a single trial — for example, a matatu cannot arrive in Nairobi and Mombasa at the same time; a Gor Mahia match cannot end in both a WIN and a DRAW. For mutually exclusive events, the addition rule states P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B). This rule does NOT apply when events can overlap (e.g., drawing a card that is both a King and a Heart). The addition rule helps decode gambling advertisements that imply bettors can simply sum their chances — but only works when the underlying events truly cannot co-occur.
summaryTablePrompt.explained: The experimental die-roll data showed P(rolling a 2 or a 5) ≈ P(rolling a 2) + P(rolling a 5) = 1/6 + 1/6 = 2/6 = 1/3. The Gor Mahia match analysis showed P(Win or Draw) = 1/3 + 1/3 = 2/3 because WIN and DRAW are mutually exclusive for one match. However, a betting advertiser who highlights 2/3 is hiding P(Lose) = 1/3 and exploiting the fact that across many independent matches, the gambler's losses accumulate — consistent with what Lessons 1–3 established about the independence of each match result.

LESSONS.aresKeywords: mutually exclusive events, addition rule probability, single chance experiment, equally likely outcomes, probability of combined events

slo.purpose: Learners apply the addition rule P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) to calculate the probability of mutually exclusive events in a single chance experiment, using a bag of mandazi-flavour tokens as the anchoring experiment.
slo.knowledge:
• Define mutually exclusive events as events that cannot occur at the same time on a single trial
• State and apply the addition rule: P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) for mutually exclusive events
• Explain why the addition rule only works when events truly cannot co-occur
• Recognise that the sum of probabilities of all mutually exclusive outcomes equals 1
slo.skills:
• Carry out a single-draw experiment with coloured tokens and record outcomes systematically
• Calculate P(A or B) using the addition rule across varied contexts (spinner, die, days of the week)
• Peer-mark worked solutions against a mark scheme and give constructive feedback
slo.attitudes:
• Show curiosity and openness when experimental results align with — or slightly deviate from — theoretical predictions
• Appreciate that the addition rule exposes the mathematical flaw in gambling claims that imply probabilities can be freely combined to guarantee wins
slo.keyInquiry: How do we apply probability in day-to-day life?
slo.purposeInStoryline: Having established in Lesson 4 that mutually exclusive events cannot co-occur and that P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B), learners now put the addition rule to work through hands-on experimentation and multiple worked contexts — moving from identifying mutually exclusive events to confidently calculating combined probabilities, and directly challenging betting-advertisement logic that misapplies probability addition.
slo.safetyNotes: No specific hazards. Ensure tokens/counters are not swallowed — remind learners these are mathematical tools, not food, even though they represent mandazi flavours.

LESSONS.overview:
This lesson is the computational payoff of the mutually exclusive events thread that began in Lesson 4. Learners move from identifying mutually exclusive events to fluently calculating combined single-chance probabilities using the addition rule P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B). The lesson is anchored in a tactile experiment: a cloth bag containing 15 coloured tokens representing three mandazi flavours sold at a school canteen — 6 plain (white), 5 coconut (yellow), and 4 cardamom (green). Each group draws one token, records the outcome, replaces it, and repeats 20 times. This mirrors a single-chance scenario: on any one draw, can you get plain AND coconut simultaneously? No — the events are mutually exclusive. This grounds the rule in physical reality before any algebra appears.

From the experiment, learners calculate P(plain), P(coconut), and P(plain OR coconut) both from their tally data and theoretically, comparing the two and discussing why slight differences arise. The teacher then leads three worked examples in escalating complexity: a spinner divided into unequal sectors (representing matatu route colours), a standard die where the event is rolling an even number OR a 5, and selecting a school day that is Monday OR Friday from the five-day week. For each, learners first attempt the problem independently for 90 seconds before the teacher reveals the solution — a structured think-before-see routine that prevents passive copying. Learners then complete a four-question independent practice set and peer-mark using a projected mark scheme.

The lesson closes by connecting the addition rule back to the driving question: gambling advertisements on Nairobi matatus and social media often imply that combining multiple bets multiplies your chances of winning. The addition rule reveals this is only mathematically valid when events are truly mutually exclusive AND when the probabilities are correctly assigned — two conditions that betting companies exploit through ambiguity. Updating the Driving Question Board and revising the cumulative class model cements the addition rule as the next permanent tool in learners' probability toolkit.

framework.learnerExperience: Each learner reads a short scenario on their ARES device or printed card: 'A school canteen sells three types of mandazi — plain, coconut, and cardamom. Amina reaches into a bag of 15 mandazi tokens without looking and pulls one out. What is the probability she gets a plain OR a coconut mandazi? Write your prediction and your reasoning before the experiment.' Learners write their prediction individually in their exercise books — including their working, not just a number — then share with a shoulder partner for 60 seconds.
framework.teacherMoves: Display the bag of tokens at the front — hold it up so learners can see it is opaque. Say: 'Before I tell you anything about what is inside, I want you to think about what we learned last lesson about the addition rule. Write your prediction now — you have 90 seconds, working alone.' [Start timer. Circulate silently. Do NOT answer questions about bag contents yet.] After 90 seconds: 'Share your prediction with your partner. You have 60 seconds — listen first, then respond.' After sharing, cold-call 3 learners with different predictions: 'Achieng, what did you predict and why?' [Wait 10 seconds.] 'Omondi, yours was different — walk us through your thinking.' [Wait 10 seconds.] 'Wanjiku, did anyone in your pair change their mind after talking? What shifted?' [Wait 12 seconds.] Do NOT confirm or correct yet. Write the three different predictions on the board under the heading 'Our Predictions — We Will Test These.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Predict-Before-Observe (PBO): By committing a written prediction to paper before any data is collected, learners activate prior knowledge from Lessons 2–4 (probability formula, mutually exclusive events, addition rule) and surface misconceptions — particularly the tendency to add probabilities without checking mutual exclusivity. Visible predictions on the board create accountability and a concrete record to revisit.
framework.formativeAssessment: Teacher scans written predictions during circulation. Key indicators: (1) Does the learner attempt to use P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B), suggesting retention from Lesson 4? (2) Does the learner correctly identify that plain and coconut are mutually exclusive on a single draw? (3) Are any learners simply guessing 50/50 or 'more than half' without calculation? Flag the third group for targeted questioning during the Observe phase.

framework.learnerExperience: Groups of 4 receive a cloth bag containing 15 coloured tokens: 6 white (plain mandazi), 5 yellow (coconut mandazi), 4 green (cardamom mandazi). One learner draws a token, the recorder notes the colour on a tally chart, the token is replaced and the bag is shaken, and the next learner draws. Groups complete 20 draws. After tallying, groups calculate three experimental probabilities: P(plain), P(coconut), and P(plain OR coconut) from their own data. Groups record results on a shared class grid drawn on the board (or projected on ARES), allowing the whole class to compare across groups.
framework.teacherMoves: Before distributing bags, say: 'I am now going to tell you what is in the bag. There are 15 tokens: 6 white for plain mandazi, 5 yellow for coconut, and 4 green for cardamom. Each group will do 20 draws with replacement. Your job is to tally each colour and then calculate three probabilities from your data.' Distribute bags and tally sheets. [Allow 6 minutes for draws.] Circulate and prompt: 'Why do we replace the token each time? What would change if we did not replace it?' [Wait 10 seconds at each group.] After draws: 'Calculate your three probabilities now — P(plain), P(coconut), P(plain OR coconut) — from your tally. You have 2 minutes.' After groups post results on the class grid, ask: 'Look at the grid. Are all groups getting exactly the same answer for P(plain OR coconut)? Why or why not?' Cold-call 2 learners: 'Kipchoge, what do you notice?' [Wait 12 seconds.] 'Fatuma, what does that tell us about experimental versus theoretical probability?' [Wait 10 seconds.] Now ask the whole class: 'Can a single token be BOTH plain AND coconut at the same time?' [Wait 5 seconds for choral response.] 'So these events are — ?' [Elicit: mutually exclusive.] 'Now let us calculate what the theory says the probability SHOULD be.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Hands-On Experiment with Class Data Aggregation: The physical draw makes mutual exclusivity viscerally real — learners cannot pull a token that is simultaneously two flavours. Aggregating group results on a shared class grid surfaces natural variation in experimental probability and motivates the need for theoretical calculation, bridging from empirical data to the formal addition rule. Connecting the tokens to mandazi — a familiar Kenyan snack — lowers affective barriers and keeps the phenomenon anchor (Gor Mahia, betting, chance) accessible.
framework.formativeAssessment: Teacher checks tally charts for systematic recording (not guessed totals). Key observable indicators: (1) Groups correctly divide tally frequency by 20 to get experimental probability — not by 15. (2) Groups sum P(plain) + P(coconut) from their tally correctly. (3) Any group reporting P(plain OR coconut) > 1 signals a calculation error — intervene immediately with: 'Can a probability ever be greater than 1? What does that tell you about your arithmetic?'

framework.learnerExperience: The teacher leads the class through the theoretical calculation for the mandazi bag, then works through three further examples on the board with increasing complexity — a spinner, a die, and days of the school week. For each example after the first, learners are given 90 seconds to attempt the problem independently in their books before the teacher reveals the solution. After all worked examples, learners complete a four-question independent practice set (displayed on ARES or the board), then peer-mark using a projected mark scheme.
framework.teacherMoves: WORKED EXAMPLE 1 — Mandazi Bag (whole class): Write on board: 'Bag: 6 plain, 5 coconut, 4 cardamom. Total = 15. One token drawn at random.' Ask: 'What is P(plain)?' [Cold-call: 'Muthoni?'] [Wait 10 seconds.] Write 6/15. 'P(coconut)?' [Cold-call: 'Otieno?'] [Wait 10 seconds.] Write 5/15. 'Are plain and coconut mutually exclusive on one draw?' [Choral: Yes.] 'So P(plain OR coconut) = ?' [Cold-call: 'Zawadi?'] [Wait 10 seconds.] Write 6/15 + 5/15 = 11/15. 'Now compare this to your experimental result from your group. Are they close? Why might they differ slightly?' [Wait 12 seconds. Take 2 hands.]  WORKED EXAMPLE 2 — Spinner (independent attempt first): Display: 'A spinner has 8 equal sectors: 3 red (Eastleigh route), 2 blue (Westlands route), 2 green (Karen route), 1 yellow (CBD route). One spin. Find P(red OR green).' Say: 'Attempt this yourself — 90 seconds, books only.' [Time.] Then cold-call: 'Amina, show us your working.' [Wait 10 seconds.] Confirm: P(red) = 3/8, P(green) = 2/8, P(red OR green) = 5/8. Ask: 'Could the spinner land on red AND green at the same time?' [Wait 5 seconds.] 'Good — that confirms mutual exclusivity.'  WORKED EXAMPLE 3 — Die (independent attempt): Display: 'A fair die is rolled once. Find P(even number OR 5).' Say: '90 seconds independently.' [Time.] Cold-call: 'Baraka.' [Wait 10 seconds.] Walk through: even = {2,4,6} so P(even) = 3/6; 5 is odd so {5} does not overlap with even; P(5) = 1/6; P(even OR 5) = 3/6 + 1/6 = 4/6 = 2/3. Ask: 'Why must we check overlap before applying the addition rule? What would go wrong if we applied it to events that CAN co-occur?' [Wait 12 seconds. Cold-call 2 learners.]  WORKED EXAMPLE 4 — Days of Week (independent attempt): Display: 'A school timetable coordinator randomly selects one day from the five school days (Monday–Friday) for a special assembly. Find P(Monday OR Friday).' '90 seconds.' [Time.] Cold-call: 'Nyambura.' [Wait 10 seconds.] Confirm: P(Monday) = 1/5, P(Friday) = 1/5, P(Monday OR Friday) = 2/5.  INDEPENDENT PRACTICE (4 questions — 5 minutes): Display on board/ARES. Q1: Bag has 4 red, 3 blue, 3 green beads. One draw. P(red OR blue) = ? Q2: A spinner has sectors: 5 orange, 3 purple, 2 white. One spin. P(orange OR white) = ? Q3: A card is drawn from cards numbered 1–10. P(prime OR 10) = ? Q4: A football match can end in Win (W), Draw (D), or Loss (L) for Gor Mahia, with P(W)=0.5, P(D)=0.25, P(L)=0.25. Find P(W OR D). After 5 minutes: 'Swap books with your partner and use the mark scheme on the board to mark. Circle any step where your partner's working is unclear — not just the answer.' Project mark scheme. Debrief Q3 especially: 'Primes from 1–10 are 2,3,5,7 — that is 4 primes. P(prime) = 4/10. Is 10 a prime? No. So are prime and 10 mutually exclusive? Yes. P(prime OR 10) = 5/10 = 1/2.'  GAMBLING CONNECTION: Ask: 'Betting apps often show odds for multiple outcomes and suggest you can combine them easily. What condition must be true before you can simply add probabilities? Are betting outcomes always mutually exclusive?' [Wait 15 seconds.] Cold-call: 'Kamau, what is the danger here?' [Wait 10 seconds.]
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Gradual Release with Independent Attempt Before Reveal (I Do → You Try → We Confirm): The teacher models the first example fully, then requires learners to attempt each subsequent example alone before seeing the solution. This prevents passive transcription and forces learners to activate the addition rule from memory. Peer-marking with a mark scheme develops metacognitive awareness — learners must evaluate mathematical reasoning, not just circle right/wrong answers. The gambling connection embeds the KICD PCI (Life Skills: Decision Making) by showing the rule has real protective value.
framework.formativeAssessment: During independent practice, teacher circulates and targets three observable errors: (1) Learner adds P(A) + P(B) without checking overlap — intervene with: 'Before you add, ask yourself: can both happen on the same trial?' (2) Learner uses total tokens as denominator inconsistently (e.g., uses 15 for one fraction and 20 for another) — redirect to: 'What is the total number of equally likely outcomes for one draw?' (3) Learner gets a probability greater than 1 — ask: 'Is that in the range we established in Lesson 3? What does that signal?' Peer-marking reveals systematic errors that teacher notes for Lesson 6.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners review the class Driving Question Board displayed at the front of the room. Working in pairs for 2 minutes, they discuss two prompts written on the board: (1) 'What new mathematical tool did we confirm today, and when can we use it?' (2) 'Does knowing the addition rule change what you think about the Gor Mahia betting advertisements?' Each pair nominates one new statement or question to add to the DQB. The class votes (thumbs up) on the three strongest additions, which are physically added to the board.
framework.teacherMoves: Direct learners to the DQB. Say: 'Look at where we started in Lesson 1 — Gor Mahia fans saying the team was due for a loss. Look at what we have added since. Today we confirmed a rule that lets us calculate combined probabilities. Discuss with your partner: what do we now know that we did not know before Lesson 5? And what new questions does this raise? Two minutes.' [Time.] Circulate and listen for: references to mutual exclusivity as a condition, questions about non-mutually-exclusive events (overlap), or questions about whether betting companies use the correct rule. After 2 minutes: 'I heard some excellent ideas. Who has a new statement for the board — something we can now say with confidence?' [Take 3–4 hands. Scribe statements.] 'Who has a new question — something today's lesson made you wonder about?' [Take 2–3 hands. Scribe questions.] Highlight any student-generated question about overlapping events (e.g., 'What if two events CAN happen at the same time?') and say: 'Hold that thought — it becomes critical in our next lessons on independent events.' Point to the driving question displayed at the top of the DQB and ask: 'Are we any closer to answering why understanding probability protects us from gambling? What would you say now that you could not say in Lesson 1?' [Wait 15 seconds. Cold-call: 'Zipporah.'] [Wait 10 seconds.]
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Driving Question Board Update (DQB Revision): The DQB functions as a living, visible record of the class's growing understanding. By revisiting it each lesson and adding only statements learners can now defend with evidence and calculation, it externalises conceptual growth and motivates the unresolved questions that drive the next lesson. Connecting today's addition rule back to the original Gor Mahia/betting phenomenon maintains the storyline thread and prevents the mathematics from feeling abstract.
framework.formativeAssessment: Teacher evaluates the quality of DQB contributions: (1) Can learners articulate the addition rule as a conditional statement ('We can add probabilities IF the events are mutually exclusive')? (2) Are learners generating questions about the limits of the rule (e.g., 'What if events overlap?'), indicating readiness for independent events in Lesson 6? (3) Does at least one learner connect the rule to the gambling/betting phenomenon unprompted? If not, the gambling connection in the Explain phase was not internalised and should be revisited at the start of Lesson 6.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners retrieve their cumulative probability model — a diagram or written framework they have been building since Lesson 1, either in their exercise books or on a shared poster. They add today's learning as a new layer: a labelled box or branch for 'Mutually Exclusive Events — Single Chance' that includes the addition rule formula, the condition for using it, and one self-chosen example. Learners annotate their model with an arrow connecting the addition rule back to the Gor Mahia / betting phenomenon with a brief written note explaining why a bettor who blindly adds probabilities may be making a mathematical error.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Take out your probability model — the diagram you have been building since Lesson 1. We are going to add one more layer today. You have 4 minutes. Add: the addition rule formula, the condition that must be met, one example you solved today, and an arrow back to the phenomenon with a sentence explaining how this rule helps someone think critically about a betting advertisement.' [Time 4 minutes. Circulate.] Look specifically for: learners who write the formula without the condition ('only when mutually exclusive') — tap their book and ask: 'What must be true first?' [Wait 8 seconds.] After 4 minutes, ask 2 learners to share their phenomenon annotation. Cold-call: 'Njoroge, read me your sentence about betting.' [Wait 10 seconds.] 'Akinyi, does your annotation agree or add something different?' [Wait 10 seconds.] Close the lesson: 'By the end of Lesson 1, we had a question: if each match is independent, why do fans believe past results change future probabilities? We now have five tools in our model. In our next lessons, we will tackle independent events directly — and see what happens when we run two experiments, not one. Keep your model safe.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Cumulative Model Revision (Layered Concept Map): The model is not redrawn each lesson but extended — each layer references and connects to prior layers, making conceptual dependencies visible. The mandatory annotation linking the addition rule to the betting/Gor Mahia phenomenon ensures every mathematical tool is contextualised within the driving question, preventing inert knowledge. Sharing annotations aloud creates a low-stakes accountability structure and allows the teacher to hear how learners are constructing the phenomenon explanation.
framework.formativeAssessment: Teacher checks that each model contains: (1) The addition rule formula written correctly: P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B). (2) An explicit condition: 'only when A and B are mutually exclusive.' (3) A phenomenon-linked annotation that goes beyond 'gambling is bad' to include mathematical reasoning (e.g., 'Adding probabilities only works if the outcomes cannot both happen — betting ads often imply you can add chances that actually overlap, making the combined probability seem higher than it really is'). Absence of the condition in (2) is the highest-priority misconception to address at the start of Lesson 6.

LESSONS.teacherReflection:
1. During the mandazi-bag experiment, did learners spontaneously identify mutual exclusivity from the physical activity, or did they only recognise it after I named it? What does this tell me about the depth of conceptual understanding from Lesson 4 — and how should I open Lesson 6?
2. In the independent practice, which of the four questions produced the most errors? Was Q3 (prime OR 10) — which required learners to first identify the set of primes — the sticking point, or was Q4 (Gor Mahia match outcomes with given probabilities rather than calculated ones) harder? How should I differentiate in Lesson 6 based on peer-marking data?
3. Did learners' DQB contributions show genuine connection between the addition rule and the gambling/betting phenomenon, or were the connections superficial (e.g., 'gambling is bad')? If superficial, which part of the Explain phase failed to land the mathematical critique of betting logic?
4. Did I give sufficient wait time (10–15 seconds) consistently, especially after higher-order questions like 'What is the danger of applying the addition rule without checking overlap?' Review the lesson mentally — were there moments I answered my own question before a learner could respond?
5. Are there learners whose cumulative models reveal a persistent gap — for example, confusing mutually exclusive events with equally likely events, or failing to apply the formula as a conditional rule? How will I provide targeted support for these learners before Lesson 6 introduces the two-event independent events chain?

summaryTablePrompt.observed: We drew coloured tokens (representing plain, coconut, and cardamom mandazi) one at a time from a bag of 15, replaced each token after drawing, and recorded 20 draws per group. We saw that no single draw could produce two flavours simultaneously — the outcomes were mutually exclusive. Our experimental probabilities for P(plain OR coconut) were close to, but not exactly equal to, the theoretical value of 11/15.
summaryTablePrompt.learned: When two events are mutually exclusive — meaning they cannot both occur on a single trial — the probability of either one occurring is found by adding their individual probabilities: P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B). This rule was confirmed across four different contexts: the mandazi bag, a matatu-route spinner, a standard die, and the school-week days. The rule only applies when events truly cannot co-occur; applying it blindly to overlapping events gives an incorrect (inflated) probability.
summaryTablePrompt.explained: Betting advertisements on Nairobi matatus and social media often imply that you can freely combine the probabilities of different outcomes to increase your chances of winning. Today's addition rule reveals this is only mathematically valid when the events are genuinely mutually exclusive and when each individual probability is correctly calculated. In a Gor Mahia match, Win, Draw, and Loss are mutually exclusive — but betting companies frequently present combinations of outcomes in ways that blur this condition, making combined probabilities appear more favourable than they truly are. This is one of the mathematical tricks that makes gambling dangerous.

LESSONS.title: Independent Events — The Coin Has No Memory
LESSONS.aresKeywords: independent events, tree diagram, sample space, multiplication rule probability, two-stage experiments

slo.purpose: Learners carry out two-stage experiments — tossing a coin AND rolling a die, then drawing a card with replacement — to derive and formalise the multiplication rule P(A and B) = P(A) × P(B) for independent events, directly explaining why a coin cannot 'remember' its last result.
slo.knowledge:
• Define independent events as events where the outcome of one trial has no effect on the outcome of another.
• State and apply the multiplication rule: P(A and B) = P(A) × P(B) for two independent events.
• Construct a complete sample space for a two-stage experiment using a tree diagram and a two-way table.
slo.skills:
• Carry out two-stage probability experiments (coin-and-die; card-draw-with-replacement) and record all outcomes systematically.
• Draw tree diagrams and two-way tables to list sample spaces and calculate probabilities of combined outcomes.
• Derive the multiplication rule from experimental frequency data and verify it against theoretical values.
slo.attitudes:
• Appreciate that mathematical independence — not luck, streaks, or fate — governs repeated chance events, building resistance to gambling fallacies.
• Demonstrate responsibility by making decisions about gambling risks using evidence from probability mathematics rather than intuition or peer pressure.
slo.keyInquiry: How do we apply probability in day-to-day life?
slo.purposeInStoryline: This lesson is the conceptual turning point of the sequence: having established equally likely outcomes (L1–L2), the range of probability (L3), and the addition rule for mutually exclusive events (L4–L5), learners now discover that when two events are independent, their joint probability is found by multiplying — and crucially, that independence means past outcomes carry zero information about future ones, mathematically dismantling the gambler's fallacy surrounding Gor Mahia's winning streak and the betting advertisements on Nairobi matatus.
slo.safetyNotes: No specific hazards. Ensure coins and die are not swallowed or thrown. If using playing cards, handle respectfully and collect all cards after the activity.

LESSONS.overview:
This lesson is the pivotal sixth instalment in the eight-lesson evidence-gathering sequence on Probability I. Having spent five lessons building the conceptual foundations — equally likely events, theoretical probability, the range 0 ≤ P ≤ 1, mutually exclusive events, and the addition rule — learners are now ready to tackle the most counterintuitive idea in the entire unit: that two events can be genuinely independent, meaning the result of the first gives absolutely no information about the result of the second. This is the mathematical reason a coin cannot be "due" for tails and Gor Mahia cannot be "due" for a loss.

The lesson is anchored in two concrete, hands-on experiments. First, learners simultaneously toss a coin AND roll a standard die — a direct two-stage experiment that mirrors the structure of the anchoring phenomenon (a football match result followed by another match result). They record all 12 possible outcomes, organise them into a tree diagram and a two-way table, compute experimental relative frequencies, and then compare these to the theoretical probabilities obtained by multiplying P(coin outcome) × P(die outcome). The Kisumu rainfall context is woven in as a supporting phenomenon: whether it rains in Kisumu today has no effect on whether a coin lands heads — two events from completely different systems are independent. Second, learners draw a card from a shuffled set of 10 numbered cards, record the outcome, replace the card, and draw again — reinforcing that replacement restores the original sample space and guarantees independence.

From these two experiments, learners derive the multiplication rule P(A and B) = P(A) × P(B) as a pattern in their own data before the teacher formalises it. The rule is then connected explicitly back to the driving question: because each football match is an independent event — just like each coin toss — Gor Mahia's seven consecutive wins do not raise or lower the probability of the eighth match's outcome by even one decimal place. The lesson closes with an update to the Driving Question Board and a revision of each learner's growing probability model.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners are shown a scenario card on the board: 'It has rained in Kisumu for the past three days. Akinyi is about to toss a coin. Does the Kisumu rain make heads more likely, less likely, or equally likely as before?' Each learner writes a private prediction in their exercise book — including a one-sentence justification — before any discussion. Then learners are shown a second scenario: 'Gor Mahia has won their last seven Premier League matches. They play Tusker FC next Saturday. Is a Gor Mahia WIN now more likely, less likely, or the same probability as it was before the streak?' Learners write a second prediction and justification. Learners hold their predictions — they will test them experimentally.
framework.teacherMoves: Write both scenarios on the board before class begins. Open with: 'Before we touch any equipment today, I want your honest gut feeling — no right or wrong answer yet.' Distribute the scenario cards or point to the board. Say: 'Read Scenario 1. Write your prediction AND your reason in your book. You have 90 seconds — go.' Allow 90 seconds of silent individual writing. After time, say: 'Now read Scenario 2. Same thing — prediction and reason. 90 more seconds.' After writing, cold-call 4 learners (aim for a mix of genders and seating positions): 'Baraka, what did you predict for the rain-and-coin scenario, and why?' Wait 10 seconds after each response before calling the next. Do NOT confirm or correct any prediction — say only: 'Interesting. Hold that thought. Our experiment today will help us check.' Record on the board a tally of how many predicted MORE LIKELY / LESS LIKELY / SAME for each scenario — keep this visible throughout the lesson.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Predict-Before-Observe (Elicitation of Prior Conceptions): By committing a written prediction to paper before any instruction, learners activate their intuitive models of probability — including the gambler's fallacy if present. The Kisumu rain contrast (clearly a different system from a coin) is designed to create productive cognitive dissonance: most learners will correctly see that rain cannot affect a coin, but then must reckon with why a football streak feels different. This dissonance is the motivating tension the experiment will resolve.
framework.formativeAssessment: Circulate during the 90-second writing windows and scan books for justifications. Look for: (a) learners who correctly predict SAME PROBABILITY for both scenarios and cite independence as a reason — they are ahead of the concept and can be asked to share their reasoning during the Explain Phase; (b) learners who predict MORE LIKELY or LESS LIKELY for the coin scenario — this flags a strong gambler's fallacy misconception that must be addressed explicitly in the Explain Phase; (c) learners who give different answers for the two scenarios (correct for coin, incorrect for football) — they sense independence in one context but not the other, which is the most common pattern and the richest teaching opportunity.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners work in groups of four. Each group receives one coin, one standard die, and a pre-printed recording table with columns: Toss Number | Coin Result (H/T) | Die Result (1–6) | Combined Outcome. Groups conduct 24 tosses of the coin-and-die together (simultaneously), recording every combined outcome. While one pair tosses and rolls, the other pair records. After 24 trials, each group lists all unique combined outcomes observed and any they did NOT observe, then constructs a tree diagram starting from the coin branch (H / T) and extending to six die branches under each, labelling all 12 possible combined outcomes (H1, H2, H3, H4, H5, H6, T1, T2, T3, T4, T5, T6). Groups also complete a two-way table with Coin (rows: H, T) against Die (columns: 1–6), placing a tick in each cell as outcomes occur. For the second experiment, groups draw from a shuffled pack of 10 numbered cards (1–10), record the number, replace and reshuffle, then draw again — repeating 20 times — recording the pair of draws each time. Learners note whether their second draw feels 'influenced' by the first.
framework.teacherMoves: Distribute materials and say: 'You are going to run two experiments today. In Experiment 1, you toss the coin and roll the die at the same time — simultaneously. Record every single result. You have 10 minutes.' Set a visible timer. After 5 minutes, pause and circulate: check that groups are recording combined outcomes (not just coin or just die separately). If a group records them separately, say: 'We need to know BOTH results together — each row is one trial with a coin AND a die result.' After 10 minutes, say: 'Now draw your tree diagram. Start with two branches — Heads and Tails. Then from each branch, draw six more branches — one for each face of the die. Label every end branch with the combined outcome like H3 or T5.' Allow 5 minutes. Cold-call one group to display their tree diagram and explain one branch: 'Group from the back row — Nafisa, trace the path to outcome T4 on your tree and tell us what it means.' Wait 12 seconds. Transition to Experiment 2: 'Now the card draw. Replace the card every time. Why do you think I said replace? Write a one-sentence hypothesis.' Allow 30 seconds, then say: 'We will come back to that.' Monitor that groups shuffle between draws. After 8 minutes total for Experiment 2, call time.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Simultaneous Multi-Representation (Tree Diagram + Two-Way Table + Frequency Data): Learners build three parallel representations of the same sample space. The tree diagram makes the sequential, branching structure of two-stage experiments visible. The two-way table organises outcomes spatially and makes it easy to count. The frequency tally from actual trials provides empirical data to compare against theoretical predictions. Using all three together prevents learners from treating any single representation as the 'real' answer and builds flexible, robust understanding of sample space.
framework.formativeAssessment: During the tree diagram construction, look for: (a) groups that draw only one level of branches — they have not grasped the two-stage structure; prompt with 'After the coin lands, the die is still rolled — what are the possible die results after Heads?'; (b) groups that list only outcomes they actually observed and omit unobserved ones — prompt with 'Your tree should show what COULD happen, not only what DID happen today'; (c) correct tree diagrams with all 12 endpoints labelled. For the two-way table, check that every cell is populated with either a tally or a zero. Ask one learner per group: 'How many different combined outcomes are possible?' — the correct answer is 12, confirming they have grasped the size of the sample space.

framework.learnerExperience: Groups use their tree diagrams to calculate the theoretical probability of each of the 12 combined outcomes. Learners first calculate P(H) = 1/2, P(T) = 1/2, and P(any specific die face) = 1/6, recording these as fractions. They then calculate P(H) × P(3) = 1/2 × 1/6 = 1/12 and compare this to the number of times 'H3' appears in their frequency table divided by 24. Groups discuss: 'What do you notice about the theoretical value 1/12 and the fraction of times H3 appeared in our experiment?' The teacher then guides the whole class to formalise the pattern as P(A and B) = P(A) × P(B), name it the multiplication rule for independent events, and define independence precisely. Learners copy the formal definition and rule into their books, then apply it to three rapid practice problems: (1) P(T and 5); (2) P(H and an even number); (3) P(drawing a '7' on the first card draw and a '7' on the second card draw with replacement). Learners also revisit the two prediction scenarios from the Predict Phase and write a correction if needed.
framework.teacherMoves: Open the Explain Phase by writing on the board: P(H) = ___ ; P(3) = ___ ; P(H) × P(3) = ___. Ask the whole class: 'Fill these in your book — 30 seconds.' After 30 seconds, cold-call a learner: 'Omondi, what is P(H) times P(3)?' Wait 10 seconds. Write 1/12 on the board. Then say: 'Now look at your frequency table. Out of 24 trials, how many times did H3 appear? Divide that by 24. Is it close to 1/12? Raise your hand if your experimental fraction is between 1/24 and 3/24 — roughly around 1/12.' Count hands. Then say: 'Every group has one of the 12 cells — on a count of three, shout out your experimental fraction for your assigned outcome. Ready? 1, 2, 3.' Listen for approximate clustering around 1/12. Then say: 'So what rule are we seeing? If I multiply the individual probabilities, I get the probability of BOTH things happening together.' Write: P(A and B) = P(A) × P(B). Say: 'This is the multiplication rule. But it only works when the events are INDEPENDENT. Independent means: knowing the result of A tells you nothing — absolutely nothing — about B. Does knowing the coin landed Heads tell you anything about what the die will show?' Wait 12 seconds. Cold-call: 'Wanjiku — yes or no, and why?' After the answer, say: 'Exactly. A coin and a die live in completely different worlds. They are independent.' Now connect to the phenomenon: 'Back to Gor Mahia. If each football match is an independent event — just like each coin toss — what does their five-win streak tell us about the probability of winning match six?' Wait 15 seconds. Cold-call 3 learners for brief responses. Close with: 'Write the formal definition of independent events and the multiplication rule in your book — leave space below to add an example in the next two minutes.' Give 2 minutes for the three rapid practice problems, then cold-call answers for each.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Concept-from-Data Formalisation (Inductive Rule Derivation): Rather than presenting the multiplication rule as a given formula, learners see it emerge from their own experimental frequencies — the fraction of times H3 appeared in 24 trials approximates 1/12, which equals 1/2 × 1/6. This inductive pathway gives the rule empirical grounding before it is stated abstractly. The strategy is strengthened by the contrast with the addition rule from Lessons 4–5: learners must now distinguish 'A or B' (addition, mutually exclusive) from 'A and B' (multiplication, independent) — a critical conceptual boundary that prevents formula confusion in assessments.
framework.formativeAssessment: Monitor the three rapid practice problems. Correct answer benchmarks: (1) P(T and 5) = 1/12; (2) P(H and even number) = 1/2 × 3/6 = 1/4; (3) P(7 then 7 with replacement) = 1/10 × 1/10 = 1/100. Flag learners who add rather than multiply — this is the most common error and indicates confusion between the addition rule (mutually exclusive, 'or') and the multiplication rule (independent, 'and'). Ask those learners: 'Are we asking for A OR B happening, or A AND B both happening?' Also check that learners who revisit their Predict Phase predictions are writing a genuine correction where needed, not simply copying a peer's answer — ask them to explain the correction in their own words.

framework.learnerExperience: Each learner writes one new sticky note (or index card) to add to the class Driving Question Board. The note must complete ONE of the following sentence starters (displayed on the board): (A) 'I now understand that a coin cannot remember its last result because…'; (B) 'The multiplication rule P(A and B) = P(A) × P(B) only works when…'; (C) 'This lesson changes my thinking about the Gor Mahia winning streak because…'; (D) 'Something I still wonder about independence is…'. Learners also update the 'What We Have Figured Out' column on the class DQB with a class-agreed statement: 'When two events are independent, knowing the result of the first event gives zero information about the result of the second. The probability of both occurring is found by multiplying their individual probabilities: P(A and B) = P(A) × P(B).' Learners physically move or annotate any earlier DQB cards that are now answered by this lesson's evidence.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Take one card from the pile on my desk. Choose ONE of the four sentence starters on the board and complete it honestly — it can be a new understanding OR a new question. Two minutes, silent writing.' After 2 minutes, ask 6 learners to read their cards aloud (select 2 from each of the first three starters and at least 1 from starter D). After each reading, say: 'Which column does this belong in — what we figured out, or what we still wonder?' Let the learner place the card. Then point to the DQB's 'What We Have Figured Out' column and say: 'Who would like to suggest a class statement summarising what we proved today?' Cold-call one learner to draft it verbally; refine as a class in 2 exchanges; write the agreed statement on a large card and add it to the board. Finally, say: 'Look at the cards we posted in Lessons 1 through 5. Are there any questions on the board that today's experiment NOW answers? Point to one if you see it.' Give 30 seconds for learners to scan the board.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Sentence-Starter DQB Update (Structured Reflection with Public Accountability): The four sentence starters are carefully designed to address different aspects of the lesson's conceptual load — the coin-memory misconception, the conditions for the multiplication rule, the phenomenon connection, and open-ended uncertainty. By requiring learners to choose and complete a starter publicly, the DQB becomes a living record of the class's growing understanding rather than a static display. Cards from Type D ('still wonder') are especially valuable as they seed the inquiry for Lessons 7 and 8.
framework.formativeAssessment: Read all posted cards before the next lesson. Cards for starters A and C should reference independence and the absence of memory/information transfer — vague answers like 'because it is random' are insufficient and indicate the learner has not yet grasped the mechanistic definition of independence. Cards for starter B should specify 'when the outcome of one event does not affect the other' — not simply 'when they are different events.' Collect any starter D cards that raise genuine new questions (e.g., 'What if the events are NOT independent — how does that change things?') and note them as potential launch points for Lesson 7.

framework.learnerExperience: Each learner returns to the probability model they have been building since Lesson 1 — a diagram or written explanation that tracks how probability works in the context of the anchoring phenomenon. Today, learners add a new labelled section titled 'Independent Events' and draw or annotate to show: (1) a two-branch tree for a two-stage experiment (e.g., Gor Mahia Match 1 outcome and Match 2 outcome); (2) the multiplication rule written symbolically and in words; (3) an arrow or annotation explicitly connecting the model to the driving question — explaining in one sentence why each match being an independent event means a winning streak carries no predictive power for the next match. Learners who finish early are invited to add a second example using the Kisumu rainfall context: P(rain today in Kisumu AND tails on a coin toss) = P(rain) × P(tails).
framework.teacherMoves: Distribute learners' model portfolios (or direct them to their model pages in their exercise books). Say: 'Open to your probability model. Today we are adding the most important layer yet. Label a new section: Independent Events.' Display the three required model elements on the board: (1) tree diagram for two-stage experiment, (2) multiplication rule in symbols and words, (3) one sentence linking independence to the driving question about Gor Mahia and gambling. Say: 'You have 5 minutes. Make it clear enough that a Form 3 student who missed today's lesson could understand your model.' Circulate and provide targeted feedback — do not correct models for learners, but ask probing questions: 'Your tree diagram shows the outcomes — now show me WHERE the 1/12 comes from on your diagram.' With 90 seconds remaining, say: 'If you have finished the required three elements, add the Kisumu rain example as a bonus.' In the final 30 seconds, ask one learner to hold up their model and narrate it to the class in two sentences. Close the lesson by pointing to the DQ written on the board and saying: 'Our driving question asks why past outcomes do not change future probabilities. What is the one-word mathematical answer we discovered today?' Wait 10 seconds. Accept 'independence' — write it on the board next to the driving question in a different colour.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Cumulative Model Revision (Progressive Model Building): The model each learner is constructing across all eight lessons serves as a personalised, cumulative explanation of the phenomenon. By adding independence as a labelled layer today — with symbolic, verbal, and diagrammatic components — learners are forced to integrate the new concept with prior model elements (equally likely outcomes, probability range, mutually exclusive events). The requirement to include a sentence linking to the driving question ensures that model building is not a mechanical diagram task but a genuine sensemaking act. The public narration at the close provides a final oral rehearsal of the key idea.
framework.formativeAssessment: Scan models for three quality indicators: (a) the tree diagram must show two full stages with all branches labelled — a single-stage tree indicates incomplete understanding of two-stage experiments; (b) the multiplication rule must appear as both P(A and B) = P(A) × P(B) and in plain language ('multiply the individual probabilities when events are independent'); (c) the driving-question sentence must use the word 'independent' and reference the absence of memory or predictive power — a sentence like 'because it is random' is insufficient. Collect models at the end of class and review overnight; use findings to inform the opening of Lesson 7, which will extend these ideas to contexts with more complex sample spaces.

LESSONS.teacherReflection:
1. During the Predict Phase, how many learners predicted the SAME PROBABILITY for both scenarios (rain-and-coin AND the football streak)? Did the learners who got both correct use the language of independence, or did they use intuition? How will I build on — or challenge — both groups in Lesson 7?

2. In the Observe Phase, did all groups successfully construct complete tree diagrams with all 12 endpoints labelled before the timer ended? If groups struggled, was the difficulty conceptual (not understanding two-stage structure) or procedural (not knowing how to draw a tree)? What scaffold would help in future lessons?

3. During the Explain Phase, how many learners added rather than multiplied when attempting the rapid practice problems? Is this confusion between P(A or B) and P(A and B) — i.e., between the addition rule from Lessons 4–5 and the new multiplication rule? What explicit contrast activity could I build into the opening of Lesson 7 to reinforce the boundary?

4. Looking at the DQB cards posted today — especially the 'still wonder' cards (starter D) — what genuine mathematical questions did learners raise? Are there questions about non-independent events, or about what happens when replacement is NOT used? How do these seeds connect to the content of Lessons 7 and 8?

5. Were learners able to articulate in their models — in their own words — why independence means that Gor Mahia's winning streak carries no mathematical information about the next match? Or did their model sentences remain vague? What additional questioning strategy could deepen this phenomenological connection before the unit concludes?

summaryTablePrompt.observed: Learners tossed a coin and rolled a die simultaneously for 24 trials, recording all combined outcomes and organising them into tree diagrams and two-way tables. They found approximately 12 equally likely combined outcomes, each occurring roughly 1/12 of the time. They also drew numbered cards with replacement and noticed the second draw was unaffected by the first.
summaryTablePrompt.learned: When two events are independent — meaning the outcome of one gives no information about the other — the probability of both occurring together is found by multiplying their individual probabilities: P(A and B) = P(A) × P(B). Independence means the first event has no memory and cannot influence the second, regardless of what that first outcome was.
summaryTablePrompt.explained: Each Gor Mahia football match is an independent event — just like each coin toss and each die roll. The five-win streak carries zero mathematical information about the probability of winning match six. The multiplication rule quantifies joint probability without any adjustment for past results, proving that the gambler's fallacy promoted in betting advertisements on Nairobi matatus is mathematically false: no streak, however long, changes the probability of the next independent event.
