LESSONS.title: Probability of Independent Events in Context: The Multiplication Rule

slo.purpose: Learners apply the multiplication rule for independent events to multi-experiment, two-outcome scenarios drawn from Kenyan daily life — rainfall in Kisumu, school demographics, and a mandazi vendor's consecutive market-day sales — and use probability evidence to critically evaluate gambling claims.
slo.knowledge: Learners will know that: (i) two events are independent when the outcome of one does not affect the probability of the other; (ii) the probability of two independent events both occurring is found by multiplying their individual probabilities, P(A and B) = P(A) × P(B); (iii) the multiplication rule extends the range-of-probability concept to compound events; (iv) the mathematical structure of independent events explains why a betting stall always profits in the long run.
slo.skills: Learners will be able to: (i) identify whether two events in a given scenario are independent; (ii) correctly apply the multiplication rule P(A and B) = P(A) × P(B) to two-experiment, two-outcome problems; (iii) calculate and interpret compound probabilities in real-life Kenyan contexts; (iv) construct and use a probability tree diagram to organise all outcomes of two independent experiments; (v) use probability calculations to construct a reasoned argument against the gambler's fallacy and gambling culture.
slo.attitudes: Learners will: (i) appreciate that mathematics provides an objective tool for evaluating everyday claims about chance; (ii) demonstrate responsibility by applying probability knowledge to protect themselves and peers from the harms of gambling; (iii) show confidence in using the multiplication rule across unfamiliar contexts; (iv) value collaborative reasoning when checking each other's probability calculations.
slo.keyInquiry: How do we apply probability in day-to-day life?
slo.purposeInStoryline: In Lesson 6 learners established mutually exclusive events and single-experiment probabilities. Lesson 7 now extends the investigation to two-experiment scenarios, directly confronting the core phenomenon: if Gor Mahia's match outcomes are independent, can we calculate the exact probability of two consecutive wins — or two consecutive losses — using multiplication? Learners also examine the mandazi vendor and spinner/stall sub-phenomenon to prove mathematically that the 'house' always wins, dismantling betting-culture claims encountered on Nairobi matatus.
slo.safetyNotes: No physical hazards. Ensure that the discussion of gambling dangers is handled sensitively — some learners may have family members affected by gambling addiction. Frame the conversation around mathematical evidence and financial protection, not personal judgment. Online safety: if learners use any digital device to access probability simulations, remind them to use only ARES-approved resources and not to share personal information.

LESSONS.overview: Learners open by revisiting the Gor Mahia phenomenon and predicting the probability that the team wins two matches in a row. Through structured calculation tasks rooted in Kenyan contexts — Kisumu rainfall, Grade 10 school demographics, and a Nairobi mandazi vendor — they discover and formalise the multiplication rule for independent events. A probability tree diagram is used as the core sensemaking tool. Learners then analyse a spinner/betting-stall scenario to calculate why the stall profits over many trials, directly linking mathematics to the dangers of gambling. The DQB is substantially updated with new mathematical claims and revised models.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners are presented with three written scenario cards (distributed or displayed on screen): Card A — 'Weather in Kisumu: the probability it rains on any given day in April is 0.7. What is the probability it rains on BOTH Monday AND Tuesday?'; Card B — 'In a Nairobi school, 60% of Grade 10 learners are female. If you pick two learners at random and independently, what is the probability BOTH are female?'; Card C — 'A mandazi vendor in Gikomba market sells out her stock with probability 0.8 on any market day. What is the probability she sells out on TWO consecutive market days?' Each learner silently records a numerical prediction for all three scenarios in their exercise book, showing their reasoning. They then share predictions with a partner (Think-Pair), comparing methods and noting disagreements.
framework.teacherMoves: Distribute or project the three scenario cards. Say: 'Before we calculate anything, I want your best mathematical guess. Write a number between 0 and 1 for each scenario AND write at least one sentence explaining how you got it. You have 4 minutes — silent, individual work.' Set a visible timer. After 4 minutes, say: 'Now turn to your partner. Compare your answers. If you disagree, explain your reasoning to each other — do not just change your answer.' Allow 3 minutes for paired discussion. Cold-call 3 pairs (one per scenario) — choose learners with visibly different predictions: 'Pair near the window — what did you predict for Card A and how did you reason?' Apply 12-second wait time before accepting responses. Record 3–4 different predictions on the board for each scenario without commenting on correctness. Ask: 'Hands up if you multiplied the two probabilities together for any of these. Hands up if you added them. Hands up if you did something else entirely.' Tally responses visibly. Say: 'By the end of this lesson you will know exactly which operation to use and why — and you will be able to check whether your prediction was correct.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Think-Pair-Share with prediction tallying. This surfaces prior conceptions (addition vs. multiplication, intuitive vs. systematic reasoning) and creates cognitive dissonance — multiple methods for the same problem. The public tally of operations (add/multiply/other) gives the teacher real-time data on the distribution of misconceptions across the class and sets up a concrete intellectual puzzle learners are motivated to resolve.
framework.formativeAssessment: Teacher circulates during silent prediction time and scans exercise books. Observable indicators of understanding: (i) learner writes a value strictly between 0 and 1 (not 'impossible' or 'certain'); (ii) learner's reasoning references both individual probabilities, not just one; (iii) learner shows some calculation attempt rather than a guess. Red flag: learner adds the probabilities (e.g., 0.7 + 0.7 = 1.4) — note this learner for targeted questioning in Phase 2.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners work in groups of four to carry out two structured activities. Activity 1 — Coin & Spinner Simulation (8 min): Each group receives (or draws) a simple two-section spinner labelled 'WIN' (probability 0.5) and 'LOSE' (probability 0.5), representing a simplified Gor Mahia match. Groups toss a coin twice (or spin twice) 20 times and record results in a two-column table (Match 1 result | Match 2 result). They tally how many times 'WIN–WIN' occurred and calculate the experimental probability. Activity 2 — Tree Diagram Construction (12 min): Learners are guided through constructing a fully labelled probability tree diagram for two independent coin tosses, showing all four branches (HH, HT, TH, TT) with probabilities written on each branch and at each endpoint. They then redraw the tree for Card A (Kisumu rain: P(rain)=0.7, P(no rain)=0.3) and record all four endpoint probabilities, verifying they sum to 1.
framework.teacherMoves: Introduce Activity 1: 'Each group — one person tosses the coin for Match 1, a different person tosses for Match 2. Record every trial in your table. You have 8 minutes.' Circulate and prompt: 'How many WIN–WIN results so far? What fraction of 20 is that?' After Activity 1, bring the class together for 2 minutes: 'Groups, call out your WIN–WIN experimental probability.' Record values on board. Say: 'They are all different — but they are all close to what value? Keep that number in mind.' Transition to Activity 2. Model the first branch of the rain tree diagram on the board: 'Monday: rain (0.7) or no rain (0.3). I draw two branches. On the rain branch — what happens on Tuesday?' Cold-call 2 learners using names: '[Name], what are the two possibilities for Tuesday if it rained Monday?' Apply 10-second wait time. Complete the tree collaboratively for the rain scenario. Then say: 'In your groups, verify that your four endpoint probabilities add to exactly 1. If they don't, find the error before moving on.' Give 4 minutes for group verification. Cold-call one group to explain their check: 'Group by the door — walk us through how you verified your tree summed to 1.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Simulation-to-structure bridging with tree diagram construction. The coin simulation provides empirical data that learners can compare against a theoretical model they then build themselves. The tree diagram is the core representational tool: it makes the sample space of two independent experiments visible, shows why probabilities are multiplied (each branch probability is conditional on the path taken), and creates a reusable template for all three scenario cards. Verifying that endpoint probabilities sum to 1 builds self-checking habits.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicators: (i) group's WIN–WIN experimental probability is in the range 0.20–0.30 (expected ~0.25); (ii) tree diagram has exactly four endpoints labelled with correct probabilities (0.49, 0.21, 0.21, 0.09 for the rain tree); (iii) endpoint probabilities sum to 1.00. Red flags: a group writes P(rain on Tuesday | it rained Monday) = 0.7 but writes a different value — suggests confusion about independence; a group's four endpoints sum to more or less than 1 — suggests branch probability errors. Teacher checks at least three groups' tree diagrams during the activity.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners formalise the multiplication rule from their tree diagrams, then apply it to all three scenario cards and to the gambling/stall analysis. Step 1 — Formalisation (5 min): Guided by the teacher, learners write the multiplication rule in their books: 'For two independent events A and B, P(A and B) = P(A) × P(B).' They verify this against their tree diagram endpoint for 'rain on both days': 0.7 × 0.7 = 0.49. Step 2 — Trio of Kenyan Contexts (12 min): In pairs, learners complete a structured worksheet solving all three scenario cards using the multiplication rule, drawing a tree diagram for each, and writing a one-sentence interpretation of each answer in plain language (e.g., 'There is a 49% chance it will rain in Kisumu on both Monday and Tuesday in April'). Step 3 — Mandazi Stall & Gambling Analysis (8 min): Learners read a short scenario: 'A betting stall near Ambassadeur Hotel, Nairobi, runs a spinner game. The spinner has 3 sectors: WIN (probability 1/3) and LOSE (probability 2/3). A player pays Ksh 20 to play. If they win, they receive Ksh 30 back (a profit of Ksh 10). If they lose, they lose their Ksh 20. Calculate: (a) P(player wins on a single spin); (b) P(player wins on BOTH of two consecutive spins); (c) If 90 learners each play twice, how much money does the stall expect to collect versus pay out?' Learners calculate individually, then compare answers with a partner.
framework.teacherMoves: Step 1 — Write on the board: 'P(A and B) = P(A) × P(B) — The Multiplication Rule for Independent Events.' Say: 'Look at your tree diagram. The probability at each endpoint is found by multiplying along the branches. This is not a coincidence — it is always true for independent events. Write this rule in a box in your book — it is one of the most important results in this unit.' Step 2 — Distribute the worksheet. Say: 'Work in pairs. For each scenario card, you must: (1) draw the tree diagram, (2) state P(A) and P(B), (3) calculate P(A and B) = P(A) × P(B), (4) write one sentence interpreting the answer for a real person who does not study mathematics.' Circulate. At the 6-minute mark, cold-call 3 different pairs (one per scenario card) to share answers: '[Name], what did you get for the mandazi vendor? What does that number mean in real life?' Apply 12-second wait time. Correct misconceptions immediately: if a learner added probabilities, ask 'Does what happened on Monday change what happens on Tuesday for the vendor? No — so these are independent. Independent means we MULTIPLY.' Step 3 — Read the stall scenario aloud. Say: 'Calculate parts (a), (b) and (c) individually — 4 minutes.' After 4 minutes, cold-call: '[Name], what is the probability a player wins both spins?' Then: '[Name], if 90 learners each play twice — that is 180 spins — how much does the stall collect? How much does it pay out? What is the stall's profit?' Work through part (c) on the board with learner input: Collect = 180 × 20 = Ksh 3,600; Expected wins = 180 × (1/3) = 60 spins; Payout = 60 × 30 = Ksh 1,800; Stall profit = Ksh 1,800. Say: 'The stall keeps Ksh 1,800 from 90 learners. This is not luck — it is mathematics. This is why gambling is dangerous.' Record this key statement on the DQB anchor strip.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Worked-example-to-application scaffolding with contextual interpretation. Learners move from abstract rule to three concrete Kenyan contexts and finally to a gambling-analysis problem. The requirement to write a plain-language sentence for each answer forces learners to connect symbolic mathematics to real-world meaning — a critical sensemaking move. The gambling stall calculation uses expected value reasoning (without formally naming it) to produce a striking numerical result (stall profits Ksh 1,800) that makes the abstract danger of gambling concrete and memorable, directly answering the driving question.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicators during pair work: (i) learner correctly identifies P(female) = 0.6 and applies P(both female) = 0.6 × 0.6 = 0.36; (ii) learner's mandazi answer is 0.8 × 0.8 = 0.64; (iii) learner's plain-language sentence accurately reflects the numerical answer without rounding errors larger than 0.01. For the stall scenario: (i) P(win both) = 1/3 × 1/3 = 1/9 ≈ 0.111; (ii) stall profit calculation correct at Ksh 1,800. Red flag: learner writes 'the stall might profit or might lose' — indicates confusion between theoretical probability and outcome certainty; redirect by asking 'Over 180 spins, what does the mathematics predict ON AVERAGE?'

framework.learnerExperience: Learners individually complete three DQB sticky notes (or written entries in their DQB section of the exercise book): (1) a CLAIM note — one new mathematical claim they can now make about independent events, supported by a calculation from today's lesson; (2) a REVISION note — one idea or prediction from an earlier lesson that today's evidence has changed or confirmed, with an explanation; (3) a QUESTION note — one new question today's lesson has raised that they still want to investigate (e.g., 'What if the events are NOT independent — does the rule change?', 'Does the stall always profit even if it has a streak of losses?'). Groups then share their CLAIM notes with the class in a 3-minute carousel, and the teacher adds three key class-agreed claims to the DQB anchor board under the heading 'Lesson 7 — Independent Events.'
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'We have one lesson left in this sequence. Before we get there, we need to update our Driving Question Board to show how our thinking has grown. You have 5 minutes to write your three notes — CLAIM, REVISION, QUESTION — individually. Be specific. Do not write 'I learned about probability.' Write a mathematical statement.' Circulate and prompt struggling learners: 'What can you NOW calculate that you could not calculate at the start of today?' After 5 minutes, facilitate the carousel: 'One person from each group — read your CLAIM note aloud in 15 seconds.' After all groups share, say: 'I am going to add three claims that came up repeatedly to our DQB.' Write: (1) 'P(A and B) = P(A) × P(B) for independent events'; (2) 'The probability of two independent events both occurring is LESS than either individual probability'; (3) 'Betting stalls are mathematically designed to profit — probability proves it.' Point to the driving question: 'Which part of our driving question can we now answer most completely?' Cold-call 2 learners. Apply 10-second wait time.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Claim-Evidence-Reasoning (CER) DQB update. The three-note structure (Claim, Revision, Question) requires learners to distinguish between what they know, what has changed, and what remains uncertain — a key epistemic sensemaking practice. The class carousel makes individual thinking public and allows the teacher to identify consensus claims versus persistent misconceptions. Anchoring new claims to the driving question maintains narrative coherence across the 8-lesson sequence.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicators: (i) CLAIM note contains a correct mathematical statement with a numerical example from today (not a restatement of the rule in isolation); (ii) REVISION note references a specific prediction or claim from a previous lesson (e.g., 'In Lesson 5 I thought past coin tosses change future ones — now I know P stays the same AND two independent flips multiply'); (iii) QUESTION note is genuinely new and mathematically meaningful, not restating today's content. Red flag: learner's CLAIM note is 'independent events do not affect each other' with no mathematical expression — prompt: 'Can you write that as a formula with numbers?'

framework.learnerExperience: Learners retrieve their cumulative probability model (begun in Lesson 1 and revised in every lesson since). Today they add a new layer to the model: a two-experiment section showing a labelled probability tree diagram for two independent events, with the multiplication rule written as a key alongside it. They annotate the model with: (a) a Kenyan context example (their choice from today's three scenario cards); (b) a statement connecting the model to the driving question — specifically, how the multiplication rule explains why the gambler's fallacy is mathematically wrong when events are independent; (c) a colour-coded arrow linking back to the 'range of probability' and 'equally likely events' sections from earlier lessons, showing how independent-event probability still obeys 0 ≤ P ≤ 1. Learners who finish early add a third experiment branch to their tree to explore what happens to compound probability as more independent events are chained.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Open your cumulative probability model. You are going to add the most powerful tool we have built so far. Draw a probability tree diagram for two independent events — use any of today's three Kenyan scenarios as your example. Label every branch and endpoint. Write P(A and B) = P(A) × P(B) as the KEY rule for this section.' Give 6 minutes for model revision. Circulate and prompt: 'Where in your model does this connect to what you drew in Lesson 1 about equally likely events?' and 'Can you show with your model exactly why someone who thinks the coin is DUE for tails is wrong?' After 6 minutes, cold-call one learner to hold up their model and describe one new feature they added today: '[Name], show us your tree diagram and explain in two sentences what it proves about independent events.' Close the lesson: 'In our final lesson we will bring ALL of this together — equally likely events, mutually exclusive events, and independent events — to answer our driving question completely. Make sure your model is ready.' Preview: 'Lesson 8 will ask: if we know all of this mathematics, why do so many people still gamble? What does probability tell us about risk over time?'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Cumulative model revision with cross-lesson annotation. Adding the multiplication rule and tree diagram to the existing model forces learners to integrate new knowledge with prior learning (range of probability, equally likely events, mutually exclusive events) rather than treating each lesson as isolated content. The explicit annotation task — connecting the model to the driving question and the gambler's fallacy — requires learners to use the model as an explanatory tool, not merely a record. This mirrors how scientists use models: as living representations that grow with evidence.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicators: (i) tree diagram has correct branch probabilities and endpoint products; (ii) multiplication rule is written as a formula (not just in words); (iii) annotation explicitly names 'independent events' and references the driving question or Gor Mahia phenomenon; (iv) colour-coded arrow to earlier model sections is present and labelled. Exit check: as learners pack up, teacher asks 3 learners at random — 'Give me one number from today's lesson and tell me what it means.' Acceptable responses include: '0.49 — the probability of rain in Kisumu on both Monday and Tuesday'; '0.64 — the probability the mandazi vendor sells out two days running'; '1/9 — the probability a gambler wins both spins of the betting stall.' If a learner cannot produce a number and meaning, note for follow-up at the start of Lesson 8.

LESSONS.teacherReflection: After the lesson, reflect on the following questions: (1) During the Predict Phase, what proportion of learners chose to add the probabilities rather than multiply? Did the cold-call pairs help surface the range of misconceptions, or did you need to draw out more voices? (2) Were the three Kenyan scenario cards sufficiently differentiated — did the rainfall and mandazi contexts feel authentic to learners, or did any group struggle to connect to the context? Consider whether alternative contexts (e.g., probability that two Rift Valley maize farmers both have a good harvest in the same season) might resonate better with your specific class. (3) Did the gambling stall calculation produce the intended 'aha' moment? If learners seemed unmoved by the Ksh 1,800 profit figure, consider whether a more locally resonant monetary amount or a peer-narrated story would strengthen the emotional impact. (4) Were all learners able to complete a full probability tree diagram by the end of the Observe Phase? If not, identify whether the gap is procedural (drawing the tree) or conceptual (knowing what probabilities to place on each branch) — these require different interventions. (5) Review the DQB QUESTION notes: do learners' new questions point naturally toward Lesson 8 content (cumulative probability, risk over time, synthesising the full driving question)? If many questions are still about basic mechanics, plan a 5-minute consolidation opener for Lesson 8.

summaryTablePrompt.observed: Learners tossed a coin (or used a spinner) twice in 20 trials and recorded WIN–WIN outcomes, finding an experimental probability close to 0.25. They constructed probability tree diagrams for two independent coin tosses and for the Kisumu rain scenario (P(rain)=0.7), labelling all four branches and verifying that endpoint probabilities summed to 1.
summaryTablePrompt.learned: Two events are independent when the outcome of one does not affect the other. The probability of both independent events occurring is found by multiplying their individual probabilities: P(A and B) = P(A) × P(B). This rule was applied to three Kenyan contexts: rain in Kisumu (0.7 × 0.7 = 0.49), two female learners selected (0.6 × 0.6 = 0.36), and a mandazi vendor selling out twice (0.8 × 0.8 = 0.64). The compound probability of two independent events is always less than either individual probability. A betting stall running 180 spins at P(win)=1/3 expects to pay out Ksh 1,800 while collecting Ksh 3,600 — a guaranteed mathematical profit of Ksh 1,800 — proving that gambling is structured to disadvantage the player.
summaryTablePrompt.explained: Because each match Gor Mahia plays is an independent event, the probability of the team winning two consecutive matches is P(win) × P(win) — not a different probability influenced by their previous results. The gambler's fallacy claims that past outcomes change future probabilities, but the multiplication rule proves this is false: each event's probability is fixed, and the compound probability of a streak is simply the product of the fixed individual probabilities. This same mathematics explains why betting stalls always profit in the long run — the game is designed so that the house's expected payout is always less than its expected collection, regardless of short-term streaks.

LESSONS.title: Consolidation, Final Explanation & DQB Closure: Why Mathematics — Not Luck — Governs the Odds

slo.purpose: To consolidate all probability concepts — equally likely events, range of probability, mutually exclusive events, and independent events — and apply them to construct a complete, mathematically grounded explanation of the anchoring phenomenon, demonstrating why the gambler's fallacy is false and why gambling is a losing proposition.
slo.knowledge: Learners know that: (a) equally likely events have equal probability; (b) probability of any event lies in the range 0 ≤ P(E) ≤ 1; (c) mutually exclusive events cannot occur simultaneously; (d) independent events have no influence on each other's probability; (e) for two independent events A and B, P(A and B) = P(A) × P(B).
slo.skills: Learners are able to: perform and interpret experiments involving equally likely, mutually exclusive, and independent events; compute probabilities of single and compound independent events; construct a written and visual explanation connecting all four probability concepts to a real-world phenomenon; evaluate gambling claims using mathematical reasoning.
slo.attitudes: Learners appreciate the role of probability in making informed, responsible real-life decisions; demonstrate responsibility by applying probability knowledge to reject gambling fallacies; show integrity when presenting peer-reviewed mathematical arguments.
slo.keyInquiry: How do we apply probability in day-to-day life?
slo.purposeInStoryline: This is the culminating lesson of the sub-strand storyline. Learners have spent seven lessons building understanding of equally likely events, the range of probability, mutually exclusive events, and independent events — all anchored to the Gor Mahia FC winning-streak phenomenon and betting culture on Nairobi matatus. In this lesson, learners synthesise every concept into a final, complete explanation: each football match is an independent event, past results cannot change future probabilities (the gambler's fallacy is mathematically false), and gambling is designed so that P(bettor wins big) approaches 0 over repeated trials. Groups present mini-posters, the Driving Question Board is formally closed, a written assessment covers all SLOs, and learners write a personal reflection on one real-life decision they will make differently using probability knowledge.
slo.safetyNotes: Discussions about gambling can be sensitive for learners whose families have been affected. Frame all references to gambling strictly as a mathematical and life-skills issue. Do not ask learners to share personal financial experiences publicly. Remind learners that the purpose of the lesson is empowerment through mathematics, not judgment of any individual or family.

LESSONS.overview: Lesson 8 is the final, consolidation lesson for Sub-Strand 3.2: Probability I. It opens with a brief return to the anchoring phenomenon — clips of Gor Mahia FC winning-streak commentary and a mock betting-app advertisement displayed on the board — to re-anchor all prior learning. In the Predict Phase, learners individually write their current best answer to the Driving Question before any group work, surfacing growth in understanding. In the Observe Phase, groups receive a structured 'Evidence Pack' containing four probability problems drawn from all four concept areas (equally likely events, range of probability, mutually exclusive events, independent events), all set in Kenyan contexts (coin tosses, a Kisumu dice game, a Nairobi lottery scratch-card, and a Gor Mahia vs AFC Leopards match sequence). In the Explain Phase, groups construct a mini-poster that mathematically answers the Driving Question, connecting all four concepts. Groups present (gallery-walk format); peers use a structured feedback card. In the DQB Closure Phase, the class reviews every question posted across the eight lessons, marks each as 'Answered — here's the math', and identifies any remaining wonderings. In the Model Building Phase, learners compare their Lesson 1 initial model with a revised final model, write a personal reflection, and complete a short written assessment covering all SLOs. The lesson closes with the teacher formally reading the KICD-mandated value statement on responsibility and decision-making.

framework.learnerExperience: Each learner receives an index card. Working individually and silently for 5 minutes, they write their current best answer to the Driving Question: 'If past outcomes of a chance event do not change future probabilities, how can we use mathematics to predict what is likely to happen, and why does this understanding protect us from the dangers of gambling?' Learners are told this is NOT a test — it is a snapshot of their thinking after eight lessons. They then share with a partner (Think-Pair) for 2 minutes before the teacher takes 3 cold-call shares. Cards are kept for comparison with Lesson 1 predictions.
framework.teacherMoves: Display the anchoring phenomenon image on the board: a split-screen of a Gor Mahia FC celebration photo alongside a photo of a matatu in Nairobi with a betting advertisement. Say verbatim: 'Eight lessons ago, this image puzzled us. Today you are going to prove — with mathematics — why the betting advertisement is misleading.' Distribute index cards. Say: 'Write your best answer to our Driving Question. Use as many probability terms as you can. You have 5 minutes — go.' Start a visible 5-minute timer. Circulate silently; do not intervene. After 5 minutes, say: 'Turn to your partner. Compare your answers. Where do you agree? Where is one of you more precise? 2 minutes.' After 2 minutes, cold-call exactly 3 learners using a name-stick draw. For each, ask: 'What ONE mathematical idea is most important in your answer?' Allow 10 seconds of WAIT TIME after each response before probing. Write key terms from responses on the board in three columns: EQUALLY LIKELY | RANGE | MUTUALLY EXCLUSIVE | INDEPENDENT. Say: 'Every term on this board is a tool you have built. Today you will use ALL of them together.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Individual Prediction Writing (Retrieval Practice): By writing a complete answer before group work, learners activate and consolidate prior knowledge across all eight lessons. The Think-Pair step surfaces vocabulary gaps before public sharing. The teacher's four-column board organiser makes the conceptual architecture of the sub-strand visible, priming learners for the synthesis task ahead.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicator: Learners' index cards use at least two probability terms correctly in a sentence connecting to the phenomenon. The teacher scans 5–6 cards during circulation and notes whether learners are linking independence to the gambler's fallacy. Cards where learners only describe equally likely events without mentioning independence signal that Phase 3 (Explain) must explicitly bridge this gap.

framework.learnerExperience: Groups of 4 receive an 'Evidence Pack' — a single A3 sheet with four worked scenarios, each requiring computation and interpretation. Scenario 1 (Equally Likely Events): A fair coin is tossed — what is P(Heads)? If it has landed on Heads 5 times in a row, what is P(Heads) on the 6th toss? Explain. Scenario 2 (Range of Probability): A Kisumu street vendor claims his lucky number will definitely appear on a 6-faced die. Write the probability of this and any event that has probability 0. Where does every real probability sit? Scenario 3 (Mutually Exclusive Events): In a single Gor Mahia vs AFC Leopards match, what is P(Gor Mahia wins AND AFC Leopards wins the same match)? Identify this as mutually exclusive. Scenario 4 (Independent Events): Gor Mahia plays three consecutive matches. Assume each match is independent and P(Gor Mahia wins) = 0.6. Calculate P(wins all three). What does this tell a bettor? Groups work for 12 minutes, recording calculations and written explanations on the Evidence Pack.
framework.teacherMoves: Distribute Evidence Packs face-down. Say: 'Do not flip until I say go.' Briefly read each scenario title aloud. Then say: 'These four scenarios cover everything we have learned. Your job is not just to calculate — it is to explain what each answer means for the person in the scenario. Flip and begin.' Set a visible 12-minute timer. Circulate using a 3-stop rotation: (1) at a group computing Scenario 4, ask: 'What does P = 0.216 mean for a person betting on all three matches?' Allow 10 seconds WAIT TIME. (2) At a group on Scenario 1, ask: 'Does the coin remember what happened before?' — pause 10 seconds — then: 'Show me in your working.' (3) At a group on Scenario 3, ask: 'Can both teams win the same match? What word describes that?' After 12 minutes, say: 'Complete your calculations. Underline the ONE sentence in each scenario that best explains the mathematics to a non-mathematician.' Cold-call 2 groups to share their underlined sentence for Scenario 4 before moving on.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Scenario-Based Evidence Analysis: Each scenario is deliberately ordered to mirror the sub-strand's conceptual progression (equally likely → range → mutually exclusive → independent), allowing learners to see how the concepts stack into a complete explanatory framework. The instruction to 'explain to a non-mathematician' shifts learners from procedural computation to genuine sensemaking, directly preparing the Explain Phase mini-poster.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicator: In Scenario 4, groups correctly compute 0.6 × 0.6 × 0.6 = 0.216 AND write a sentence explaining that even a 60% chance per match gives only a ~22% chance of winning all three, illustrating why repeated betting is a losing strategy. Groups that calculate correctly but write no explanation need targeted prompting in Phase 3. Groups that multiply incorrectly (e.g., add probabilities) require immediate re-teaching of the multiplication rule for independent events.

framework.learnerExperience: Each group uses a large sheet of paper (A2 or flip-chart) to construct a mini-poster that answers the Driving Question in full. The poster must include: (a) a title restating the Driving Question in their own words; (b) one worked example for each of the four concepts, all using Kenyan contexts from the Evidence Pack or their own; (c) a clear written explanation of the gambler's fallacy using the word 'independent'; (d) a mathematical argument for why gambling is a losing proposition (using the multiplication rule for independent events); (e) a probability line (0 to 1) with at least three events from the phenomenon placed on it. Groups have 15 minutes to build the poster, then conduct a Gallery Walk: posters are displayed around the room, one group member stays as 'explainer' while the other three walk. Walkers use a structured feedback card with two prompts: 'The strongest mathematical argument on this poster is ___' and 'One thing that could be more precise is ___'. After 8 minutes of walking, groups reunite, read feedback, and make one revision to their poster in a different colour.
framework.teacherMoves: Before groups begin, display the poster requirements on the board and say verbatim: 'Your poster must make a mathematician AND a Standard 8 pupil both understand why the matatu betting ad is misleading. Use numbers, words, and a probability line.' Set a 15-minute timer. During construction, circulate and use targeted probing at 3 groups: (a) 'Where is the word INDEPENDENT on your poster — and why does it matter?' (b) 'Your probability line — where would you place P(Gor Mahia wins every match for 10 games in a row)? Calculate it.' (c) 'What is the difference between mutually exclusive and independent? Can you show both on one poster?' After gallery walk, bring the class together. Say: 'I am going to read three posters' gambler's fallacy explanations aloud without naming the group. Vote with thumbs — which is most mathematically precise?' Read 3 excerpts. After each, allow 10 seconds WAIT TIME before thumbs. Announce the most precise and explain why, using KICD language: 'Independent events have no influence on each other's probability — that is the mathematical truth the betting industry hopes you forget.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Gallery Walk with Structured Feedback Cards: The gallery-walk format externalises group thinking for peer critique, which is a high-leverage sensemaking strategy because learners must evaluate mathematical precision in others' arguments — a skill that deepens their own understanding. The 'revision in a different colour' step makes the improvement process visible and models scientific revision of explanations. The teacher's anonymous reading of three gambler's fallacy explanations creates a whole-class norm-setting moment that closes the conceptual arc of the sub-strand.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicator: Mini-posters include a correct, written statement of the form 'Because each match is an independent event, P(win) = 0.6 regardless of previous results' AND a correct multiplication calculation showing how probability decreases across consecutive independent bets. Feedback cards that only reference visual design rather than mathematical content indicate learners are not yet evaluating conceptual precision — the teacher should redirect by asking: 'Point to the calculation. Is it correct? Is the explanation complete?'

framework.learnerExperience: The full DQB (constructed and added to across all 8 lessons) is displayed. Each group receives three sticky dots: green (answered fully), yellow (partially answered), red (still wondering). Working as a class, learners go question by question. For each question, the teacher reads it aloud and asks: 'Has our learning answered this? Who can point to the evidence — on a poster, in their notes, or in today's Evidence Pack?' Learners place their dots. Questions that receive all green dots are ceremonially 'closed' by the teacher drawing a tick and writing the key mathematical answer beside them in one sentence. Questions receiving red dots are acknowledged as productive wonderings that point beyond Grade 10 (e.g., conditional probability, expected value). The Driving Question itself is read aloud by the whole class in unison, then the teacher cold-calls 3 individual learners to each give one sentence of the answer, building a class composite final answer that is written on the board.
framework.teacherMoves: Stand at the DQB. Say: 'This board has been our scientific record for 8 lessons. Every question on it came from YOUR curiosity about Gor Mahia and the matatu betting ads. Let's see how far our mathematics has taken us.' Read the first question. Pause 10 seconds. Ask: 'Green, yellow, or red — dot it.' After all questions are dotted, focus on any red-dot questions. Say: 'These are not failures — they are invitations. The mathematics you will study in Grade 11 and 12 will answer them.' Write beside each red-dot question: 'See: conditional probability / expected value — Grade 11.' For the Driving Question closure, say: 'Everyone read the Driving Question with me — together.' Lead the unison read. Then say: 'I need three voices to build our final answer. [Name 1], give me the first sentence — about equally likely events and independence.' WAIT 10 seconds. '[Name 2], add a sentence about the range of probability and what it tells a bettor.' WAIT 10 seconds. '[Name 3], close it — why is gambling mathematically a losing proposition?' Write the three-sentence composite answer on the board. Say: 'This is our class's final answer. Copy it into your notes.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: DQB Dot Voting and Composite Answer Construction: The dot-voting protocol makes the class's collective epistemic progress visible — learners can literally see how many of their original questions are now answered with mathematics. The composite three-sentence final answer, built from three cold-called voices, models the scientific practice of constructing explanations from evidence and is deeply connected to NGSS SEP 6 (Constructing Explanations). Writing it on the board and in notes creates a durable record of consolidated understanding.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicator: The three cold-called learners each produce a grammatically complete, mathematically accurate sentence that uses at least one probability term correctly and references the phenomenon. If a called learner produces a vague sentence (e.g., 'probability means chance'), the teacher probes: 'Can you add a number or a formula to make that more precise?' and allows 10 additional seconds of WAIT TIME before scaffolding.

framework.learnerExperience: Part A — Model Comparison (8 min): Learners retrieve their Lesson 1 initial model (a drawing/diagram of what they thought governed football match outcomes). They draw a revised Final Model beside it, incorporating all four probability concepts, the independence of each match, the probability line, and the gambler's fallacy label. They annotate with arrows showing what changed and why. Part B — Written Assessment (20 min): Learners complete a short individual written assessment (5 questions) covering all SLOs: (1) Compute P(equally likely event) in a dice scenario; (2) Place three events on a probability line and justify; (3) Identify two mutually exclusive events from a Kenyan football context; (4) Calculate P(independent events) across two trials using a coin and a Gor Mahia match; (5) Write 3 sentences explaining why the gambler's fallacy is mathematically false. Part C — Personal Reflection (5 min): On the back of the assessment paper, learners complete: 'One real-life decision I will make differently because of what I now know about probability is ___, because mathematically ___.'
framework.teacherMoves: Distribute Lesson 1 model sheets (collected earlier in the unit). Say: 'Look at what you thought 8 lessons ago. Now draw your final model beside it. Use colour — red for what you now know was wrong, green for what you now know is mathematically true.' Set 8-minute timer. Circulate, noting 3 learners whose models show the most dramatic conceptual growth — affirm verbally and privately: 'This revision shows real mathematical thinking.' After model comparison, collect models and distribute assessment papers. Say clearly: 'This is individual work. No group discussion. You have 20 minutes. Use every probability term we have learned. Show all working.' Set timer. Circulate silently for the first 5 minutes, then stop and stand at the front. For Question 5 (gambler's fallacy explanation), after 10 minutes say: 'If you are stuck on Question 5, look at the composite answer on the board — but write it in YOUR own words.' After assessments are collected, say: 'Flip your paper. One minute of silence. Think of one real decision — buying a scratch-card, betting on a match, playing a game of chance. Now write your reflection. This is for you.' Allow 5 minutes. Close the lesson by reading verbatim from KICD: 'The learner makes correct decisions on life issues that involve gambling using the knowledge of probability.' Say: 'That is what you have done today. That is mathematics in service of your life.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Model Comparison (Initial vs. Final): Placing the Lesson 1 model and Final Model side by side makes the learner's conceptual growth concrete and visible — a metacognitive strategy that research consistently links to deep learning. The colour-coded annotation (red = corrected misconception, green = new understanding) makes the revision process explicit rather than implicit. The personal reflection connects mathematical knowledge to agency and decision-making, fulfilling the KICD PCI of Life Skills (Decision Making) and the value of Responsibility.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicators for Written Assessment: (Q1) Correct probability fraction with sample space shown. (Q2) Three events correctly placed with P = 0, 0 < P < 1, and P = 1 each represented. (Q3) Two events named that genuinely cannot occur simultaneously (e.g., 'Gor Mahia wins AND loses the same match'). (Q4) Correct multiplication of two independent probabilities (e.g., 0.5 × 0.6 = 0.3) with working shown. (Q5) Three sentences that include the word 'independent', a statement that past outcomes do not change future probability, and a reference to the phenomenon. Learners who score below 3/5 are flagged for a 15-minute catch-up session using the Evidence Pack scenarios as remediation tools.

LESSONS.teacherReflection:
After the lesson, reflect on the following questions and record your notes:
1. CONCEPTUAL GROWTH: Compare three learners' Lesson 1 models with their Final Models. What is the most common misconception that PERSISTED despite eight lessons? (Common residual error: learners may still confuse 'independent' with 'mutually exclusive' — if so, plan a 10-minute re-teach opener for the next strand using a Kenyan context, e.g., drawing a card from a deck vs. tossing a coin simultaneously.)
2. DQB QUALITY: Were there questions on the DQB that received red dots (unanswered)? List them. Do they suggest gaps in your instructional sequencing, or are they genuinely beyond Grade 10 scope? Plan how to explicitly bridge these to Grade 11 content in your end-of-unit notes to learners.
3. ENGAGEMENT WITH GAMBLING PCI: Did the personal reflection task (Part C) reveal any learners whose family context involves gambling? If so, consult the school counsellor. The mathematics of probability is a powerful protective tool — ensure the framing remained empowering, not shaming.
4. ASSESSMENT DATA: Tally scores on Q4 (independent events multiplication) and Q5 (gambler's fallacy explanation). If more than 30% of learners score 0 on Q5, the verbal/written explanation skill was under-practised across the unit — plan more 'explain to a non-mathematician' tasks in future sub-strand sequences.
5. GALLERY WALK FEEDBACK CARDS: Review the structured feedback cards collected from the gallery walk. Did learners evaluate mathematical precision or only surface features (neatness, colour)? If the latter, model mathematical peer feedback explicitly at the start of the next unit.
6. KICD VALUES CHECK: Did the closing statement — reading the KICD value of Responsibility aloud — feel authentic in your classroom context? If learners responded with recognition (nodding, quiet), it landed. If it felt formal, consider asking a learner to read it next time to increase ownership.

summaryTablePrompt.observed: Learners worked through four Kenyan-context probability scenarios (coin toss independence, Kisumu dice range, mutually exclusive football match outcomes, and a three-match independent-event multiplication), recorded calculations and written explanations on an Evidence Pack, and conducted a gallery walk critiquing peer mini-posters using structured feedback cards.
summaryTablePrompt.learned: Each football match (and every chance event studied) is an independent event — its probability is fixed and cannot be changed by past outcomes. The gambler's fallacy is mathematically false because P(event) for an independent trial does not depend on previous results. Gambling is a losing proposition because the multiplication rule for independent events shows that P(winning multiple consecutive bets) decreases sharply with each additional trial. All probability values lie in the range 0 ≤ P(E) ≤ 1, and mutually exclusive events (both teams winning the same match) have a combined probability of zero.
summaryTablePrompt.explained: Using all four probability concepts together — equally likely events, range of probability, mutually exclusive events, and independent events — learners constructed a complete written and visual explanation of why the Gor Mahia winning-streak debate and the Nairobi matatu betting advertisements are both examples of the gambler's fallacy. The composite class answer, the mini-posters, the DQB closure, and the written assessment all demonstrate that mathematics — not luck, streaks, or intuition — governs the odds, and that this knowledge is a practical tool for responsible decision-making in real life.

FINAL_EXPLANATION.subjectLabel: Essential Mathematics Grade 10 – Sub-strand 3.2 Probability I: Final Explanation
FINAL_EXPLANATION.instructions: Answer all five questions in the space under each prompt. Remember the puzzle we began with: during the 2023 Kenyan Premier League season, fans said Gor Mahia FC was 'due' for a loss after a winning streak, while betting advertisements on Nairobi matatus and social media told youth they could 'beat the odds'. Use what you learned in Lessons 1 to 8: your coin, die and token experiments, the probability formula, the range of probability, mutually exclusive events and independent events. Show all working, write probabilities as fractions in their simplest form, and explain your reasoning in full sentences. Where a question says 'suppose', use the numbers given for that question only.

sections.title: Part 1: Does the past change the chance? (Equally likely events)
sections.prompt:
In our class experiment, each pair tossed a 10-shilling coin 40 times and we pooled the results. A fan at a Nairobi bus stage says: 'A coin has landed on heads five times in a row, so tails is now more likely.'
(a) What is the theoretical probability of heads on one toss of a fair coin? Show how you get it using the formula.
(b) Is the fan correct? Explain your answer using what you know about how one toss relates to the next.
(c) Why did pooling the whole class's results give a more reliable estimate of the probability than your own pair's 40 tosses?
(d) Name the mistake in thinking that the fan, and the fans who said Gor Mahia was 'due' for a loss, are making.
sections.exemplar:
(a) P(heads) = number of favourable outcomes ÷ total number of equally likely outcomes = 1 ÷ 2 = 1/2 (0.5 or 50%).
(b) No. Each toss is an independent event: the result of one toss gives no information about the next. A coin has no memory, so after five heads the probability of tails on the next toss is still 1/2, exactly the same as the probability of heads.
(c) A larger sample gives a more reliable estimate. One pair's 40 tosses can drift away from 1/2 by chance, but when many pairs' results are pooled these chance differences tend to even out and the experimental probability gets closer to the theoretical 1/2.
(d) This is the gambler's fallacy: believing that past outcomes change the probability of future independent events. Each match Gor Mahia plays is treated as an independent event, so the earlier wins do not change the probability of the next result. The fans who say the team is 'due' for a loss are wrongly treating the next match as if it depends on the earlier wins.

sections.title: Part 2: Computing probabilities from the mandazi bag (Equally likely outcomes and the range of probability)
sections.prompt:
A cloth bag at a school canteen holds 15 tokens that represent mandazi flavours: 6 plain (white), 5 coconut (yellow) and 4 cardamom (green). One token is drawn at random.
(a) Calculate P(plain), P(coconut) and P(cardamom) as fractions in simplest form.
(b) Add the three probabilities. What does your total tell you about the possible outcomes of one draw?
(c) Write down one event for this bag that has probability 0, and one that has probability 1.
(d) A betting advertisement claims '120% chance of winning'. Using the range of probability, explain whether this claim can be true.
sections.exemplar:
(a) P(plain) = 6/15 = 2/5. P(coconut) = 5/15 = 1/3. P(cardamom) = 4/15.
(b) 6/15 + 5/15 + 4/15 = 15/15 = 1. The three flavours cover every possible outcome of one draw, so one of them is certain to happen. The probabilities of all the individual outcomes add up to 1.
(c) Probability 0 (impossible): drawing a red token, since the bag has no red tokens (P = 0/15 = 0). Probability 1 (certain): drawing a token that is not red, since every token in the bag is white, yellow or green (P = 15/15 = 1).
(d) No. Every probability must satisfy 0 ≤ P ≤ 1. 120% is the same as 1.2, which is greater than 1, so it is mathematically impossible. No winning streak or advertisement can push a probability outside this range.

sections.title: Part 3: Mutually exclusive events and the addition rule
sections.prompt:
(a) Use the mandazi bag from Part 2. Are the events 'draw a plain mandazi' and 'draw a coconut mandazi' mutually exclusive on a single draw? Explain what mutually exclusive means.
(b) Calculate P(plain or coconut) for one draw and show your rule.
(c) In our token experiment each group drew 20 times with replacement. Why might a group's experimental result for 'plain or coconut' be close to, but not exactly equal to, your answer in (b)?
(d) Suppose that, for one Gor Mahia match, we assume P(Win) = 1/3 and P(Draw) = 1/3 and that Win, Draw and Loss are the only possible results. (Real matches need not have equal chances; use these numbers for this question only.) Calculate P(Win or Draw). Then explain why a betting advertisement that only talks about 'Win or Draw' could mislead a bettor, and state when the addition rule must not be used.
sections.exemplar:
(a) Yes. Mutually exclusive events cannot both happen on a single trial. One draw gives only one token, so it cannot be both plain and coconut.
(b) For mutually exclusive events, P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B). So P(plain or coconut) = 6/15 + 5/15 = 11/15.
(c) The experimental probability is based on only 20 draws, and chance causes small differences from the theoretical value. With more draws the experimental result would get closer to 11/15.
(d) Win and Draw cannot both happen in one match, so they are mutually exclusive and P(Win or Draw) = 1/3 + 1/3 = 2/3. Since the three results cover everything, P(Loss) = 1 − 2/3 = 1/3. An advertisement that highlights 2/3 hides this remaining probability of a Loss, the outcome where the bettor loses. The addition rule must not be used when events can happen together (overlap), because adding would count the overlap twice and give an inflated probability. It also only gives correct answers when each individual probability has been correctly found.

sections.title: Part 4: Independent events, the multiplication rule and why the stall always wins
sections.prompt:
(a) Suppose that for each match the probability that Gor Mahia wins is 1/3 (an assumed value for this question), and each match is independent. Calculate the probability that Gor Mahia wins two matches in a row, and then three matches in a row. Show the rule you use.
(b) Gor Mahia has just won seven matches in a row. A fan says the probability of winning the eighth match must now be different from 1/3. Use the idea of independent events to respond.
(c) A betting stall in Nairobi charges Ksh 20 per spin. A player wins Ksh 30 whenever the spinner lands on the winning sector, and P(win) = 1/3 on each spin. Over 180 spins, a win is expected on about 1/3 of the spins. Using this, work out the money you would expect the stall to collect, the money you would expect it to pay out, and the profit you would expect. Explain what this shows about gambling.
sections.exemplar:
(a) For independent events, P(A and B) = P(A) × P(B). Two wins in a row: 1/3 × 1/3 = 1/9. Three wins in a row: 1/3 × 1/3 × 1/3 = 1/27. The probability of a longer streak gets smaller with each extra match.
(b) The fan is wrong. Each match is an independent event, just like each coin toss, so the seven-match streak carries no information about match eight. The probability of winning the eighth match is still the same fixed 1/3. The streak does not raise it or lower it.
(c) Collected: 180 × Ksh 20 = Ksh 3,600. Expected number of wins: 1/3 × 180 = 60. Expected payout: 60 × Ksh 30 = Ksh 1,800. Expected profit for the stall: Ksh 3,600 − Ksh 1,800 = Ksh 1,800. This is what we expect on average over many spins, not a guarantee for any short run: a player can have a lucky streak, but over many spins the stall is expected to collect more than it pays out. The player wins only 1/3 of the time yet pays Ksh 20 every spin, so the game is set up to disadvantage the player, and gambling is a losing proposition.

sections.title: Part 5: Answering the Driving Question
sections.exemplar: Mathematics lets us say what is likely, not what will certainly happen. Independence does not stop us doing this: each trial has a fixed probability, and we can calculate it and compare it with results over many trials. For equally likely outcomes we use P(event) = favourable outcomes ÷ total outcomes, for example P(heads) = 1/2 for a fair coin, and our pooled class data supported this because larger samples give more reliable estimates. Every probability lies between 0 and 1, so an advertisement claiming '120% odds' or a commentator saying a streak makes a win 'inevitable' is mathematically impossible. When outcomes are mutually exclusive, such as Win, Draw and Loss in one Gor Mahia match, we add their probabilities, but advertisements that stress only the favourable combination, like P(Win or Draw), hide the probability of losing. Most importantly, each match is an independent event, so a coin or a team has no memory: the probability of the next match stays fixed no matter how long the winning streak is. The fans who said Gor Mahia was 'due' for a loss, and bettors who think tails is 'due' after five heads, are making the gambler's fallacy. The multiplication rule shows that the probability of winning several bets in a row gets smaller with each extra bet, so long winning streaks are unlikely. In our stall example, the stall expected to collect Ksh 3,600 and pay out Ksh 1,800 over 180 spins, so it expects a profit, although short runs can differ. Understanding this protects me because I will not trust betting advertisements that promise I can 'beat the odds', and I will not spend my money chasing a 'due' win. Instead I will use probability to make careful and responsible decisions.

SUMMARY_TABLE.drivingQuestion: DRIVING QUESTION: If past outcomes of a chance event — like a coin toss or a football match — do not change future probabilities, how can we use mathematics to predict what is likely to happen, and why does this understanding protect us from the dangers of gambling?

lessons.title: Anchoring Phenomenon & Equally Likely Events: Is Gor Mahia "Due" for a Loss?
lessons.observed: Learners tossed a 10-shilling coin 40 times per pair, recorded outcomes in a tally table, and pooled class results to compare experimental probability with the theoretical value of P(Heads) = ½.
lessons.learned: Each coin toss is an independent equally likely event. Theoretical probability = (favourable outcomes) ÷ (total equally likely outcomes). Past outcomes do NOT change future probability — a coin has no memory — directly contradicting the gambler's fallacy promoted in betting advertisements seen on Nairobi matatus and social media.
lessons.explained: The Gor Mahia fan's claim that the team is 'due' for a loss is an example of the gambler's fallacy. Mathematics shows that if each event is independent and equally likely, its probability remains fixed regardless of previous outcomes. Our coin-toss data supported the theoretical P = 0.5, especially when the whole class's results were pooled — showing that larger samples give more reliable estimates of true probability.

lessons.title: Computing Probability of Equally Likely Outcomes
lessons.observed: Learners rolled a six-faced die 60 times per group and drew tokens from a bag of githeri-coloured tokens (white/maize, brown/beans, green/peas), recording all outcomes in tally tables and computing experimental probabilities as fractions, decimals, and percentages.
lessons.learned: Learners derived the theoretical probability formula P(event) = number of favourable outcomes ÷ total number of equally likely outcomes, and applied it to Kenyan contexts: selecting a name from a class of 30 learners, and drawing a coloured token from a mixed bag. They confirmed that all individual outcome probabilities for a fair die sum to 1.
lessons.explained: Learners explained, using the probability formula and the concept of equally likely outcomes, why Gor Mahia FC's past winning streak does not change the probability of the next match result — directly challenging the gambler's fallacy promoted in Nairobi betting advertisements.

lessons.title: Range of Probability: From Impossible to Certain
lessons.observed: Learners analysed Kenyan scenario Evidence Cards (maize kernels, fruit bowls, dice, spinners) and the class's accumulated coin-toss data from Lesson 1 to find probabilities and place them on a number line.
lessons.learned: The probability of any event must satisfy 0 ≤ P(event) ≤ 1; P = 0 means impossible (e.g., snow in Kisumu in July); P = 1 means certain (e.g., sunrise over Mombasa); all other events fall strictly between 0 and 1, and no winning streak — including Gor Mahia's — can push a future probability outside these bounds.
lessons.explained: Learners used the range of probability to refute a fictional gambling advertisement claiming '120% odds', and wrote a mathematical explanation of why a sports commentator claiming Gor Mahia's winning streak raises their probability above 1 is mathematically impossible, using the boundary rule 0 ≤ P ≤ 1.

lessons.title: Mutually Exclusive Events — Identification & The Addition Rule
lessons.observed: Learners sorted 10 Kenyan-context event-cards into 'mutually exclusive' and 'not mutually exclusive' piles, justifying each placement. They also rolled a die 30 times each and recorded experimental frequencies for Event A (rolling a 2), Event B (rolling a 5), and Event A or B (rolling a 2 or a 5), pooling class data on the board.
lessons.learned: Mutually exclusive events are events that cannot occur simultaneously on a single trial — for example, a matatu cannot arrive in Nairobi and Mombasa at the same time; a Gor Mahia match cannot end in both a WIN and a DRAW. For mutually exclusive events, the addition rule states P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B). This rule does NOT apply when events can overlap (e.g., drawing a card that is both a King and a Heart). The addition rule helps decode gambling advertisements that imply bettors can simply sum their chances — but only works when the underlying events truly cannot co-occur.
lessons.explained: The experimental die-roll data showed P(rolling a 2 or a 5) ≈ P(rolling a 2) + P(rolling a 5) = 1/6 + 1/6 = 2/6 = 1/3. The Gor Mahia match analysis showed P(Win or Draw) = 1/3 + 1/3 = 2/3 because WIN and DRAW are mutually exclusive for one match. However, a betting advertiser who highlights 2/3 is hiding P(Lose) = 1/3 and exploiting the fact that across many independent matches, the gambler's losses accumulate — consistent with what Lessons 1–3 established about the independence of each match result.

lessons.title: Probability of Single-Chance Mutually Exclusive Events — The Addition Rule in Action
lessons.observed: We drew coloured tokens (representing plain, coconut, and cardamom mandazi) one at a time from a bag of 15, replaced each token after drawing, and recorded 20 draws per group. We saw that no single draw could produce two flavours simultaneously — the outcomes were mutually exclusive. Our experimental probabilities for P(plain OR coconut) were close to, but not exactly equal to, the theoretical value of 11/15.
lessons.learned: When two events are mutually exclusive — meaning they cannot both occur on a single trial — the probability of either one occurring is found by adding their individual probabilities: P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B). This rule was confirmed across four different contexts: the mandazi bag, a matatu-route spinner, a standard die, and the school-week days. The rule only applies when events truly cannot co-occur; applying it blindly to overlapping events gives an incorrect (inflated) probability.
lessons.explained: Betting advertisements on Nairobi matatus and social media often imply that you can freely combine the probabilities of different outcomes to increase your chances of winning. Today's addition rule reveals this is only mathematically valid when the events are genuinely mutually exclusive and when each individual probability is correctly calculated. In a Gor Mahia match, Win, Draw, and Loss are mutually exclusive — but betting companies frequently present combinations of outcomes in ways that blur this condition, making combined probabilities appear more favourable than they truly are. This is one of the mathematical tricks that makes gambling dangerous.

lessons.title: Independent Events — The Coin Has No Memory
lessons.observed: Learners tossed a coin and rolled a die simultaneously for 24 trials, recording all combined outcomes and organising them into tree diagrams and two-way tables. They found approximately 12 equally likely combined outcomes, each occurring roughly 1/12 of the time. They also drew numbered cards with replacement and noticed the second draw was unaffected by the first.
lessons.learned: When two events are independent — meaning the outcome of one gives no information about the other — the probability of both occurring together is found by multiplying their individual probabilities: P(A and B) = P(A) × P(B). Independence means the first event has no memory and cannot influence the second, regardless of what that first outcome was.
lessons.explained: Each Gor Mahia football match is an independent event — just like each coin toss and each die roll. The five-win streak carries zero mathematical information about the probability of winning match six. The multiplication rule quantifies joint probability without any adjustment for past results, proving that the gambler's fallacy promoted in betting advertisements on Nairobi matatus is mathematically false: no streak, however long, changes the probability of the next independent event.

lessons.title: Probability of Independent Events in Context: The Multiplication Rule
lessons.observed: Learners tossed a coin (or used a spinner) twice in 20 trials and recorded WIN–WIN outcomes, finding an experimental probability close to 0.25. They constructed probability tree diagrams for two independent coin tosses and for the Kisumu rain scenario (P(rain)=0.7), labelling all four branches and verifying that endpoint probabilities summed to 1.
lessons.learned: Two events are independent when the outcome of one does not affect the other. The probability of both independent events occurring is found by multiplying their individual probabilities: P(A and B) = P(A) × P(B). This rule was applied to three Kenyan contexts: rain in Kisumu (0.7 × 0.7 = 0.49), two female learners selected (0.6 × 0.6 = 0.36), and a mandazi vendor selling out twice (0.8 × 0.8 = 0.64). The compound probability of two independent events is always less than either individual probability. A betting stall running 180 spins at P(win)=1/3 expects to pay out Ksh 1,800 while collecting Ksh 3,600 — a guaranteed mathematical profit of Ksh 1,800 — proving that gambling is structured to disadvantage the player.
lessons.explained: Because each match Gor Mahia plays is an independent event, the probability of the team winning two consecutive matches is P(win) × P(win) — not a different probability influenced by their previous results. The gambler's fallacy claims that past outcomes change future probabilities, but the multiplication rule proves this is false: each event's probability is fixed, and the compound probability of a streak is simply the product of the fixed individual probabilities. This same mathematics explains why betting stalls always profit in the long run — the game is designed so that the house's expected payout is always less than its expected collection, regardless of short-term streaks.

lessons.title: Consolidation, Final Explanation & DQB Closure: Why Mathematics — Not Luck — Governs the Odds
lessons.observed: Learners worked through four Kenyan-context probability scenarios (coin toss independence, Kisumu dice range, mutually exclusive football match outcomes, and a three-match independent-event multiplication), recorded calculations and written explanations on an Evidence Pack, and conducted a gallery walk critiquing peer mini-posters using structured feedback cards.
lessons.learned: Each football match (and every chance event studied) is an independent event — its probability is fixed and cannot be changed by past outcomes. The gambler's fallacy is mathematically false because P(event) for an independent trial does not depend on previous results. Gambling is a losing proposition because the multiplication rule for independent events shows that P(winning multiple consecutive bets) decreases sharply with each additional trial. All probability values lie in the range 0 ≤ P(E) ≤ 1, and mutually exclusive events (both teams winning the same match) have a combined probability of zero.
lessons.explained: Using all four probability concepts together — equally likely events, range of probability, mutually exclusive events, and independent events — learners constructed a complete written and visual explanation of why the Gor Mahia winning-streak debate and the Nairobi matatu betting advertisements are both examples of the gambler's fallacy. The composite class answer, the mini-posters, the DQB closure, and the written assessment all demonstrate that mathematics — not luck, streaks, or intuition — governs the odds, and that this knowledge is a practical tool for responsible decision-making in real life.
